complexity.Application: Concept must be applied to a concrete scenario to pick the right answer

questions.question: Your application needs to process 10,000 independent, non-urgent requests (an overnight classification run) where a turnaround of a few hours is acceptable. What is the most appropriate integration approach?

options.A: Send all requests synchronously in a tight loop as fast as possible
options.B: Use the Message Batches API to submit the requests as a batch job at a lower cost
options.C: Open one long-lived streaming connection for all requests simultaneously
options.D: Manually shard the requests across multiple API keys to bypass rate limits

questions.explanation: The Message Batches API is designed for large volumes of non-latency-sensitive requests and offers reduced cost compared to synchronous calls.

questions.question: You are translating a product requirement — 'a real-time chat feature' — into a technical integration plan. Which factor should most directly influence your choice between synchronous (real-time) calls and the Batches API?

options.A: The programming language used by the frontend
options.B: Whether the use case requires an immediate response (latency-sensitive) or can tolerate delayed, asynchronous processing
options.C: The number of engineers on the team
options.D: Whether the application uses TypeScript or Python

questions.explanation: Latency sensitivity is the key driver: real-time, user-facing interactions need synchronous calls; bulk/delay-tolerant work suits the Batches API.

questions.question: Roughly what cost reduction does the Message Batches API offer relative to equivalent synchronous requests?

options.A: No reduction; batching only changes latency
options.B: About 10%
options.C: About 50%
options.D: About 90%

questions.explanation: Batch processing is priced at roughly half the cost of the equivalent synchronous calls, which is the main reason to choose it for delay-tolerant volume.

questions.question: You submit a batch and need to match each result back to the row of your database that produced it. What mechanism supports this?

options.A: You must submit one request per batch to keep the mapping unambiguous
options.B: Results are returned in exactly the submission order, so you can zip them positionally
options.C: You re-send the original prompt text and match on string equality
options.D: Each request carries a caller-supplied custom identifier that is echoed on its result

questions.explanation: Each request in a batch carries a caller-assigned identifier that comes back attached to the corresponding result, so results can be reassociated without relying on ordering.

questions.question: A batch has been submitted but not all requests have finished. What is true of the results?

options.A: Nothing is retrievable until every request in the batch reaches a terminal state
options.B: The batch is automatically cancelled if any single request fails
options.C: Partial results are streamed back continuously as each request completes
options.D: Failed requests silently disappear from the result set

questions.explanation: A batch is retrieved once processing has ended; individual requests reach terminal states and the results become available as a set rather than as a live stream.

questions.question: Select the TWO scenarios that are appropriate for the Message Batches API.

options.A: Generating the reply in a live chat widget while the user waits
options.B: Re-classifying a 400,000-row archive of historical support tickets overnight
options.C: Generating bulk tags and summaries for a data warehouse refresh that runs nightly
options.D: Streaming a token-by-token response into a code editor's autocomplete

questions.explanation: Batch suits high-volume, delay-tolerant work such as re-classifying a historical archive or annotating records for a nightly refresh. A live chat reply and token-by-token autocomplete are latency-critical and interactive, so they need a synchronous or streaming request.

questions.question: Which statement about Message Batches API timing is accurate?

options.A: Batches never expire
options.B: Most batches finish within an hour; a batch that has not finished within 24 hours expires, and results remain downloadable for 29 days
options.C: Results are deleted as soon as they are downloaded once
options.D: Every batch completes in under one minute

questions.explanation: Batches trade latency for a 50% discount and throughput. Unfinished requests at 24 hours come back as 'expired' and are not billed.

questions.question: In a batch result set, some entries have result types errored, canceled or expired. How are those billed?

options.A: They are billed at the full synchronous rate
options.B: The whole batch is billed whether or not requests succeed
options.C: They are not billed; only succeeded requests are charged
options.D: They are billed at double the batch rate

questions.explanation: Only succeeded requests incur charges. Handle each type explicitly, and resubmit errored or expired requests where appropriate, keyed by custom_id.

questions.question: A batch shares a large system prompt across 50,000 requests. Why might prompt caching hit less often than in synchronous traffic, and what helps?

options.A: Caching is impossible inside batches
options.B: Batches require a different model
options.C: Batches automatically cache everything for free
options.D: Batch processing can take longer than the 5-minute default cache lifetime, so the 1-hour cache TTL improves hit rates on shared prefixes

questions.explanation: The batch discount and cache pricing stack, but requests in a batch may be processed far apart in time. Using the 1-hour TTL on the shared prefix keeps entries alive across that spread.

questions.question: What does enabling citations on a document content block allow an application to do?

options.A: Compress the document to reduce token usage
options.B: Automatically translate the document into another language
options.C: Convert the document into an image for vision processing
options.D: Ground specific claims in Claude's response back to precise locations in the source document, enabling traceable, source-linked answers

questions.explanation: Citations ground specific claims back to precise source locations, enabling traceable, source-linked answers.

questions.question: How does the citations feature differ from simply instructing Claude in the prompt to 'cite your sources'?

options.A: Prompt-based citation instructions are always more reliable than the citations feature
options.B: There is no difference; both produce identical guarantees
options.C: Citations is a structured, API-level feature tied to the document content block that grounds claims to specific source locations, rather than relying on the model to informally mention a source in free text
options.D: Citations can only be used with images, never documents

questions.explanation: Citations is a structured, API-level grounding mechanism, distinct from and more reliable than an informal prompt instruction to 'cite sources.'

questions.question: A compliance tool needs every factual claim in Claude's output to be traceable to an exact location in the source regulatory document. Which feature is most directly suited to this requirement?

options.A: The Batches API
options.B: Extended thinking
options.C: The citations feature on the document content block
options.D: Prompt caching

questions.explanation: Citations is purpose-built for grounding claims to exact source locations, matching this compliance requirement directly.

questions.question: Which application would benefit LEAST from enabling citations?

options.A: A compliance-review tool grounding findings in regulatory text
options.B: A legal research tool needing to show exactly where in a case file a claim came from
options.C: A research assistant summarizing a scientific paper with source-linked claims
options.D: A casual creative-writing brainstorming assistant with no source documents involved

questions.explanation: Citations only add value when there's a source document to ground claims in; a source-free creative brainstorming task has nothing to cite.

questions.question: What is a reasonable design choice for an application when citations are enabled and Claude's response includes several grounded claims?

options.A: Citations cannot be surfaced to end users under any circumstances
options.B: Prevent the user from ever seeing which document a claim came from
options.C: Surface the citation information to the end user (e.g., as inline references or links back to the source location) so they can verify claims
options.D: Discard the citation information entirely and show plain text only

questions.explanation: Surfacing citation data to end users (inline references, source links) is the natural way to realize citations' verifiability benefit.

questions.question: An application enables citations on its document blocks and also requests a JSON response through structured outputs (output_config.format). What happens?

options.A: The citations are embedded inside the JSON automatically
options.B: Citations are silently dropped and the JSON is returned
options.C: Structured outputs is ignored and plain cited text is returned
options.D: The request is rejected with a 400, because citations and structured outputs are incompatible

questions.explanation: Citations interleave cited text blocks with source locations, which conflicts with a schema-constrained response, so the combination returns a 400. Choose one: citations when traceability is the requirement, structured outputs when a program consumes a fixed shape.

questions.question: A compliance team needs every assertion in a generated summary to be traceable to an exact location in the source filing. Which approach best meets this?

options.A: Append 'always cite your sources' to the system prompt and parse the model's freeform references
options.B: Enable the citations feature on the document content block and render the returned source locations
options.C: Ask for a bibliography at the end of the response
options.D: Lower temperature so the model quotes the document more literally

questions.explanation: Citations is an API-level feature on the document block that returns structured references to precise source locations, which is verifiable in a way that prompt-level instructions are not.

questions.question: What distinguishes the citations feature from simply instructing the model to cite its sources?

options.A: Citations works without providing any source document
options.B: Citations returns structured references tied to the supplied document rather than model-generated prose references
options.C: Citations is only available in batch mode
options.D: Citations replaces the need to validate output entirely

questions.explanation: The feature yields structured, machine-readable references anchored to the document you supplied, which is why they can be displayed and checked; prompt-level requests produce prose that may itself be fabricated.

questions.question: When citations are enabled on a plain-text document, how does the response identify each cited passage?

options.A: An HTTP header listing page numbers
options.B: Nothing; citations are only visible in the console
options.C: A footnote list appended as free text at the end
options.D: Cited text blocks carry a citations array with the cited_text, the document index, and a location such as character indices (page numbers for PDFs)

questions.explanation: Citations are structured and machine-readable: char_location for plain text, page_location for PDFs, content_block_location for custom content. That is what lets an app render verifiable links.

questions.topic: Code Review, Testing & CI for LLM Features
questions.question: A team adds a CI test that compares each Claude response to a stored 'golden' string and fails on any difference. What happens over time?

options.A: It reliably catches every regression
options.B: It reduces token cost
options.C: It fails on correct-but-reworded answers, generates noise, and gets disabled, leaving the system less covered than before
options.D: It makes the model deterministic

questions.explanation: Outputs vary between identical runs, so literal comparison reports wording changes rather than regressions. Use scored evaluation against a versioned set with a threshold, plus contract tests on schemas and parsers.

questions.topic: Code Review, Testing & CI for LLM Features
questions.question: Select the TWO pipeline stages that suit a Claude-backed service.

options.A: Automatically rewriting the prompt and redeploying whenever an eval score drops
options.B: A scored evaluation against a versioned dataset, with a pass threshold
options.C: Exact string comparison of every response against a stored output
options.D: Contract tests that check output schemas and the downstream parsers that consume them

questions.explanation: A stage earns its place if it catches real regressions and stays green when a correct answer is reworded. Literal comparison fails the second test; automatic remediation deletes the signal a human was meant to act on. A token/cost regression check is a good third stage.

questions.topic: Code Review, Testing & CI for LLM Features
questions.question: A pull request adding a Claude feature hardcodes the model name and API settings, has no error handling for rate limits, and includes no tests. What should the reviewer do?

options.A: Approve it because the feature works in the demo
options.B: Request only tests, since they would reveal the other problems
options.C: Approve it and fix the gaps in a follow-up commit of their own
options.D: Request all three fixes before merge, since each gap fails independently in production

questions.explanation: Hardcoded configuration needs a deploy to change, a missing error path turns the first rate limit into an unhandled exception, and no tests leave both unverifiable. Fixing only the largest gap is wrong by the same rule as fixing none.

questions.topic: Code Review, Testing & CI for LLM Features
questions.question: Prompts in a codebase are edited directly in production config, and nobody can say which wording was live last Tuesday. What is the fix?

options.A: Treat prompts as code: one home in version control, a tracked history, and review no weaker than the code's
options.B: Keep a hand-maintained change log in a wiki
options.C: Freeze all prompt edits permanently
options.D: Store prompts only in the model's context window

questions.explanation: A prompt is behaviour-defining code; two prompt versions are two different systems on the same input. A manual log matches reality only while somebody maintains it.

questions.topic: Code Review, Testing & CI for LLM Features
questions.question: An automated code-review bot comments on every pull request. The team assumes risky changes are now blocked. What is wrong with this assumption?

options.A: Automated reviews cannot read code
options.B: A reviewer produces findings; a merge gate is something you build by reading its findings (for example, severity) in your own pipeline and deciding what stops a merge
options.C: Bots always block merges on their own
options.D: Findings from bots are legally binding

questions.explanation: A managed review can post inline comments and a check run that never blocks on its own. Treating the reviewer's presence as a gate converts a signal meant for a human into nothing.

questions.topic: Code Review, Testing & CI for LLM Features
questions.question: Which properties make a change easy to review?

options.A: It bundles several unrelated features to save review time
options.B: It is as large as possible so the reviewer sees full context
options.C: It does one thing, shows an example of it running, includes a test proving the behaviour, and states what it assumes about its environment
options.D: It omits tests because the reviewer can run the code

questions.explanation: A reviewer forced to reconstruct intent reviews last and catches least. Small, single-purpose changes with evidence and stated assumptions get reviewed well.

questions.topic: Code Review, Testing & CI for LLM Features
questions.question: A scripted Claude Code job produces different results on a developer laptop and the CI runner. What is the most likely cause and fix?

options.A: Claude Code randomises output on CI
options.B: CI runners use a different model by default
options.C: Laptops have faster internet
options.D: Non-interactive runs load whatever hooks, settings, skills and MCP servers the host has configured; run with explicit configuration (for example, a bare mode that skips discovery) so every machine behaves the same

questions.explanation: A run that loads whatever the host happens to have is not reproducible. State the context explicitly and skip local discovery for jobs that must behave identically everywhere.

questions.question: What does a dateless model ID such as claude-sonnet-4-6 (and later) refer to?

options.A: A model that is retrained weekly
options.B: One fixed model snapshot that stays constant for that ID's lifetime; an updated model ships under a new ID
options.C: Whatever the newest Sonnet happens to be
options.D: A random model chosen per request

questions.explanation: From the 4.6 generation the dateless ID is canonical and pinned. Earlier models carried a snapshot date, and their short aliases advanced to the newest snapshot of that minor version.

questions.question: A regression appeared after a week in which the model ID, two prompts and a plugin version all changed, and none of the changes were recorded. What does this situation lack, and what fixes it?

options.A: A faster upgrade cadence so everything is always latest
options.B: More logging of model outputs
options.C: Attributability: make every behaviour-deciding input (model ID, prompt version, plugin versions, configuration) explicit and pinned in tracked configuration so changes can be attributed and rolled back
options.D: Removing the plugin that most recently changed

questions.explanation: The span between the last reproducible state and now holds every unrecorded change. Pinning creates the record, rollback is what it buys, and an upgrade cadence records nothing.

questions.question: A team pins an exact model ID. Can observable behaviour still change?

options.A: No; a pinned ID guarantees byte-identical outputs forever
options.B: Only if the team changes the prompt
options.C: Only if the API key is rotated
options.D: Yes; weights are fixed per ID, but routing, safety classifiers and serving logic can change, so pinning bounds the variables rather than removing them

questions.explanation: Pinning holds the model steady, not the whole serving stack. That is another reason to keep an evaluation baseline running against production.

questions.question: Why keep the previously pinned model ID available in configuration after upgrading?

options.A: So a regression can be handled by rolling back to a known-good value instead of an emergency hotfix
options.B: Because the API requires two model IDs per request
options.C: To halve token costs
options.D: Because old IDs never retire

questions.explanation: Half the value of pinning is having a rollback target, and it is the half most often skipped.

questions.question: Each environment (dev, staging, prod) runs a different model, prompt version and plugin set, and nobody can say why. What is the right fix?

options.A: Unpin everything so the environments converge on latest
options.B: Consolidate into tracked configuration that declares each environment's deliberate differences
options.C: Hardcode configuration into application code
options.D: Make all environments identical at all times

questions.explanation: Environments differ on purpose; the fix is to declare the differences where they can be read back. Configuration in application code forces a release for every settings change.

questions.question: A Claude Code plugin your team depends on changed behaviour overnight, though nothing in your repository changed. What prevents a repeat?

options.A: Disable all plugins
options.B: Fork and copy the plugin into every repository
options.C: Declare a version constraint for the plugin dependency so it resolves within a tested range instead of tracking the newest release
options.D: Read the plugin's release notes every morning

questions.explanation: An unpinned dependency tracks latest, so an upstream tag changes your behaviour with no commit and no record. A version constraint holds it in a tested range.

questions.question: A feature has been edited in place for months and its evaluation set predates current traffic. The team wants to improve it. What comes first?

options.A: Delete the stale evaluation set
options.B: Rewrite the prompts from scratch
options.C: Upgrade to the newest model immediately
options.D: Restore measurability: pin the inputs, version the prompts as they stand, and rebuild the evaluation set from recent traffic

questions.explanation: Improvement without a baseline cannot be judged. Rewriting discards what the feature has learned, and deleting the stale set leaves less than nothing.

questions.question: A prompt is shared by four downstream applications. A change is proposed. What must happen before rollout?

options.A: Assess the effect of the change on each consumer, then coordinate the rollout based on what that assessment finds
options.B: Ship it to two consumers now and the rest later
options.C: Announce the change in a channel and ship it
options.D: Ship it to staging; a clean staging run is the assessment

questions.explanation: Announcing, scheduling and staging are communication, not assessment. Shipping to some consumers leaves one system answering under two versions.

questions.question: Select the TWO items that belong in version control for a Claude-backed service.

options.A: Prompt text, model identifiers and output schemas
options.B: Evaluation datasets and their pass thresholds
options.C: API keys and other credentials
options.D: Each developer's machine-specific local settings

questions.explanation: Anything whose change changes production behaviour belongs in version control. Credentials never do, and machine-specific settings are deliberately excluded.

questions.question: Who is responsible for maintaining conversation history (prior turns) across multiple calls to the Messages API?

options.A: History can only be maintained using the Batches API
options.B: History is never needed since Claude has persistent memory across all API calls by default
options.C: The calling application, which must include the full relevant message history in each request
options.D: Anthropic's servers automatically persist and inject full history for you

questions.explanation: The Claude API is stateless between calls; the application must resend the conversation history it wants considered on each request.

questions.question: The Messages API is stateless. What follows for a multi-turn chat application?

options.A: The application must resend the relevant prior turns with each new request
options.B: The API retains the last ten turns per API key automatically
options.C: State is preserved as long as the same model is used
options.D: Conversation history is stored server-side and referenced by conversation id

questions.explanation: Because the endpoint holds no session state, the caller owns the history and must include the prior turns it wants the model to condition on.

questions.question: A long-running assistant thread is approaching the model's context limit. Which strategy preserves continuity most economically?

options.A: Drop the system prompt to free room for more conversation
options.B: Truncate the most recent turns, since older context is more authoritative
options.C: Start a fresh conversation with no carryover on every request
options.D: Summarize older turns into a compact recap and keep recent turns verbatim

questions.explanation: Compacting distant history into a summary while retaining recent turns verbatim keeps the salient state within budget. Dropping the system prompt or the newest turns discards the most load-bearing context.

questions.question: In a tool-using conversation, what must the application include when continuing after the model requests a tool call?

options.A: A fresh conversation seeded with just the tool output
options.B: The tool result with a newly generated identifier of the caller's choosing
options.C: Only the tool's output, with the assistant turn omitted
options.D: The assistant turn containing the tool request, followed by a user turn carrying the matching tool result

questions.explanation: The assistant's tool-request turn stays in the history and is answered by a result block whose identifier matches the request, so the model can tie the output to the call it made.

questions.question: A team ports an older integration that ended every request with a partially written assistant turn (a prefill such as '{') to force JSON. What happens on Claude 4.6 and later models?

options.A: The prefill is silently ignored and the response is unaffected
options.B: The request is rejected with a 400 invalid_request_error, so the format must be enforced another way, such as structured outputs or system prompt instructions
options.C: The model repeats the prefill verbatim and then stops
options.D: The prefill resets the system prompt

questions.explanation: Prefilling the final assistant turn is not supported on Claude 4.6 and later models; the API returns a 400 telling you the conversation must end with a user message. Use structured outputs (output_config.format) to guarantee a JSON shape, or state the format in the system prompt.

questions.question: Two users of a chat product occasionally see fragments of each other's conversations. Which application-side defect best explains this?

options.A: Conversation history is being kept in a process-wide structure rather than scoped per session
options.B: The model's context window is too small for concurrent use
options.C: The API is leaking state between requests sharing an API key
options.D: Streaming was enabled for both sessions simultaneously

questions.explanation: Since the API holds no state, cross-talk originates in the application's own history storage — typically history held in shared or global scope instead of per-session.

questions.question: When extended thinking is enabled for a request, which statement is accurate?

options.A: Extended thinking replaces the need for a system prompt
options.B: Thinking is free because the reasoning is never shown to the user
options.C: The model can reason before its final answer, and those thinking tokens are billed as output tokens and count toward max_tokens
options.D: Extended thinking eliminates all token costs for the response

questions.explanation: Thinking happens before the final answer and is billed as output tokens whether or not the reasoning text is displayed. Display settings (such as an omitted or summarized thinking view) change visibility, not cost.

questions.question: On current Claude models (Claude 4.6 and later), how is the depth of thinking on a request primarily controlled?

options.A: It cannot be influenced; the model decides unilaterally
options.B: With adaptive thinking plus the effort parameter (low, medium, high and above), which trades thoroughness against token spend
options.C: By selecting a dedicated reasoning-only endpoint
options.D: By raising temperature until reasoning appears

questions.explanation: Adaptive thinking lets the model decide how much to think, and output_config.effort sets how much it spends. The older fixed budget_tokens setting is deprecated on the 4.6 models and rejected with a 400 on newer ones, so effort is the dial to reach for. Temperature is unrelated, and non-default sampling values are themselves rejected on Claude 4.7 and later.

questions.question: A team runs every request in a high-volume classification pipeline at the highest effort level, and costs rise sharply with no accuracy gain. What is the most reasonable conclusion?

options.A: High effort is incompatible with classification and returns invalid output
options.B: Effort should be raised further to see a benefit
options.C: The cost increase is unrelated to effort and must come from caching
options.D: Thinking tokens are billed, and simple pattern-matching tasks rarely benefit from extra deliberation, so effort should be tuned down for this route

questions.explanation: Reasoning tokens are billed like other output, so maximum effort on a task that does not need deliberation adds cost without quality benefit. Effort is tuned per route against an eval: classification and chat often do well at low effort, while coding and long agentic work repay higher settings.

questions.question: Which task profile is the strongest candidate for extended thinking?

options.A: Extracting a phone number from a fixed-format record
options.B: Reconciling a multi-step financial calculation with interacting constraints
options.C: Translating a single sentence into French
options.D: Echoing a supplied string in uppercase

questions.explanation: Deliberation pays off where the answer depends on several interacting steps that benefit from working through. Mechanical single-step transformations gain nothing.

questions.question: When continuing a tool-use conversation in which extended thinking was enabled, how should the prior thinking content be handled?

options.A: Rewrite the thinking blocks into a shorter paraphrase
options.B: Strip all thinking blocks before sending the next request
options.C: Preserve the returned thinking blocks in the conversation history as they were received
options.D: Move the thinking content into the system prompt

questions.explanation: Thinking blocks are returned as part of the assistant turn and are passed back unmodified when continuing the exchange, so the model retains the reasoning that led to its tool request.

questions.question: Where does extended thinking output appear in a response?

options.A: In an HTTP header
options.B: Interleaved silently into the text block with no marker
options.C: Only in the usage object as a token count
options.D: As a distinct content block preceding the final text

questions.explanation: Reasoning is returned as its own content block ahead of the answer, which is what lets an application choose whether to display, log, or hide it.

questions.question: A research assistant fetches web pages and passes them to Claude. Where should the fetched content go?

options.A: In tool_result blocks, labelled with their source and delimited, with the policy that supplied content never overrides instructions stated in the system prompt
options.B: Into a tool_result block together with the developer's standing instructions
options.C: Appended to the developer's own instructions in the same text block
options.D: Concatenated into the system prompt so the model definitely reads it

questions.explanation: Authority follows the channel. Persistent rules go in the system prompt, the user's own request in the user turn, and third-party content in tool results. Your own instructions never belong in a tool result, because content there is treated as untrusted.

questions.question: An operator needs to switch a running conversation into 'terse mode' without invalidating the cached prefix. On models that support it, what is the cleanest mechanism?

options.A: Put the instruction inside the most recent tool_result
options.B: Append a mid-conversation system message to the messages array rather than editing the top-level system prompt
options.C: Ask the user to type the instruction themselves
options.D: Edit the top-level system prompt on the next request

questions.explanation: A mid-conversation system message carries operator authority, cannot be the first message, and appends after the cached history, so the prefix stays intact. Editing top-level system invalidates the cache from that point on.

questions.question: The same guidance behaves well in Claude Code's terminal but poorly when the team calls the Messages API directly. Why?

options.A: The API uses a weaker model
options.B: The terminal runs at a higher temperature
options.C: Interfaces differ in what is already in context: the API is stateless and supplies nothing, while Claude Code adds its own system prompt and project context, so the rule must be stated on each channel
options.D: The API ignores system prompts

questions.explanation: The raw API sees only what you send. The Agent SDK defaults to a minimal prompt, and Claude Code adds full working context. A rule the application depends on must be stated once per channel it relies on.

questions.question: A pipeline extracts facts from a contract and then writes a customer-facing summary, all in one call with one output schema. Quality is uneven between the two parts. What should change?

options.A: Raise the token limit on the combined call
options.B: Lower the temperature
options.C: Add 'be thorough' to the prompt
options.D: Split them into separate calls, each with its own output contract and its own evaluation

questions.explanation: Stages judged by different standards of success need separate calls with separate schemas. The token-cost argument for merging them leaves quality out of the comparison.

questions.question: A downstream service keeps breaking on JSON that is well formed and schema-valid. What is the most likely design mistake?

options.A: The schema describes what a good answer looks like instead of what the consumer needs, and it is versioned on the producer's schedule rather than the consumer's
options.B: The consumer should loosen its parser until it passes
options.C: The JSON is too short
options.D: The model should return XML instead

questions.explanation: A schema is a contract with the model, the consumer and the platform. Write it from the consumer's needs and version it on the consumer's schedule.

questions.question: Why is project guidance in CLAUDE.md or similar instruction files not enough to guarantee an action never happens?

options.A: Instruction files are encrypted and unreadable
options.B: Instruction files load as context that shapes decisions; only a deterministic check that runs first, such as a hook or a permission rule, removes the option
options.C: Instruction files are only read in plan mode
options.D: Instruction files are ignored entirely

questions.explanation: Context shifts probability; a gate decides. Whenever a requirement contains the word 'never', ask which component would have to fail for the outcome to occur.

questions.question: Which statement about sending base64-encoded images to Claude via the Messages API is accurate?

options.A: Base64-encoded images cannot be included in a Messages API request under any circumstances
options.B: Base64-encoded images require a completely separate, non-Messages API endpoint
options.C: Base64-encoded images can only be sent using the deprecated Completions API
options.D: Base64-encoded images can be included as typed image content blocks within a message, alongside text

questions.explanation: An image block's source can be inline base64 data (with a media type), a URL, or a file_id from the Files API. It sits in the message content alongside text blocks.

questions.question: Which statement about sending PDF documents to Claude via the Messages API is accurate?

options.A: PDF documents can be included as typed document content blocks within a message, alongside text
options.B: PDF documents require a completely separate, non-Messages API endpoint
options.C: PDF documents can only be sent using the deprecated Completions API
options.D: PDF documents cannot be included in a Messages API request under any circumstances

questions.explanation: PDFs are sent as document content blocks (base64, URL, or Files API file_id). Each page is processed both as extracted text and as an image, so page count drives token cost.

questions.question: A support app re-sends the same 40-page PDF manual on every turn of a long conversation. Which approach avoids re-uploading the bytes each time?

options.A: Paste the manual into the system prompt as plain text on every request
options.B: Convert the PDF to images and send those instead
options.C: Upload it once with the Files API and reference it by file_id in a document block (and cache the prefix if it is resent often)
options.D: Send the manual only on the first turn; the API remembers it for the session

questions.explanation: The Files API lets you upload once and reference the file by file_id in later requests. The API is still stateless, so the reference must appear in every request that needs it, and prompt caching is what stops you paying full input price for the repeated tokens.

questions.question: A developer wants Claude to analyze a screenshot of a UI bug. What is the correct way to include this in a Messages API request?

options.A: As an image content block (e.g. base64-encoded) within the same message alongside any accompanying text
options.B: As a separate, unrelated API call using a different endpoint entirely
options.C: By embedding a URL directly in the system prompt text with no special formatting
options.D: Images cannot be analyzed by Claude under any API configuration

questions.explanation: Vision input is provided as typed image content blocks within a message, which can be combined with text blocks in the same request.

questions.question: An invoice-processing service receives scanned PDFs and must extract line items. What is the most direct integration?

options.A: Send the PDF as a document content block in the same Messages request as the extraction instruction
options.B: Run a separate OCR service first, since the API accepts text only
options.C: Convert the PDF to a spreadsheet before sending it
options.D: Call a dedicated document endpoint distinct from Messages

questions.explanation: PDFs are supplied as document content blocks alongside the text instruction in an ordinary Messages request; there is no separate document endpoint.

questions.question: Select the TWO accurate statements about multimodal requests.

options.A: Multiple images can be included in a single message alongside text
options.B: Images must be sent to a separate vision endpoint before the text request
options.C: Only one content block of any type is permitted per message
options.D: Image content blocks may be supplied as base64-encoded data

questions.explanation: Messages accept several content blocks of mixed types, and images can be provided as base64 data. There is no separate vision endpoint, and messages are not limited to a single block.

questions.question: Image-heavy requests in a document pipeline are consuming far more tokens than expected. Which factor most directly explains this?

options.A: Image dimensions drive token consumption, so large images cost substantially more than downscaled ones
options.B: Base64 encoding is billed at double the rate of binary upload
options.C: Only the file name is tokenized, so cost should be negligible
options.D: Images are billed per request rather than per token, so volume is irrelevant

questions.explanation: Claude reads images in 28x28-pixel patches, so an image costs about ceil(width/28) x ceil(height/28) visual tokens, up to the model's resolution cap (images above it are downscaled first, which caps the cost). Below that cap, larger images cost more, so downscaling to the smallest size that keeps the detail you need is the main lever on cost. Encoding method and file name do not change the token count.

questions.question: A 300-page scanned PDF costs far more tokens than its file size suggests. Why?

options.A: PDFs are billed per megabyte
options.B: Only the first page is billed
options.C: Each PDF page is processed as both extracted text and an image, so page count drives cost more than file size
options.D: Scanned PDFs are billed at double the output rate

questions.explanation: Because pages are rendered as well as read, a long document is expensive regardless of compression. Send only the pages the task needs.

questions.question: You are building a customer support widget that must handle a static 5,000-token system prompt on every request while user input varies. What should you do to reduce latency and cost?

options.A: Send the system prompt as a separate API call before each user turn
options.B: Enable prompt caching on the static system prompt content
options.C: Truncate the system prompt to 500 tokens
options.D: Switch to synchronous polling instead of a single request

questions.explanation: Prompt caching lets repeated static content (like a large system prompt) be reused across calls without being reprocessed and re-billed at full price each time.

questions.question: How do the costs of a cache write and a cache read compare to an ordinary uncached input token?

options.A: A write costs somewhat more than an uncached token; a read costs a small fraction of one
options.B: A write is free and a read is billed at the full rate
options.C: Both cost the same as an uncached token; only latency improves
options.D: Both are cheaper than an uncached token

questions.explanation: Establishing the cache carries a premium over normal input pricing, while subsequent reads of that prefix are billed at a small fraction, which is why caching only pays off when the prefix is reused.

questions.question: Caching was enabled on a large system prompt, but the hit rate is near zero. The prompt ends with the current timestamp. What is the problem?

options.A: The timestamp changes the cached prefix on every call, so no request matches a stored one
options.B: Caching cannot be applied to system prompts
options.C: Timestamps are stripped automatically, so the cause must lie elsewhere
options.D: The cache requires the whole request, not just a prefix, to be identical

questions.explanation: A cache hit needs an exact prefix match. Volatile content inside the cached span invalidates it every call; such content belongs after the cache breakpoint.

questions.question: Where should a cache breakpoint be placed in a request containing tool definitions, a long static system prompt, and a short variable user question?

options.A: Between the tool definitions and the system prompt only
options.B: After the tool definitions and system prompt, before the user question
options.C: After the user question, at the end of the request
options.D: At the very start of the request, before the tool definitions

questions.explanation: The breakpoint goes at the end of the stable span so tools and the static system prompt are cached while the varying question stays outside the cached prefix.

questions.question: How can an application confirm that prompt caching is actually taking effect?

options.A: By enabling streaming, which emits a cache-hit event
options.B: Caching is opaque and cannot be observed from the response
options.C: By comparing wall-clock latency across runs, the only available signal
options.D: By reading cache creation and cache read token counts reported in the response usage data

questions.explanation: Usage data reports tokens written to and read from the cache, which is the direct measurement of whether the breakpoint is working.

questions.question: A cached prefix stops being reused after a quiet period in a low-traffic application. What explains this?

options.A: Low traffic increases the minimum cacheable length
options.B: Cache entries expire after a period of inactivity
options.C: Caches persist indefinitely, so the cause must be a prompt change
options.D: Caches are invalidated whenever the API key is used from a new IP

questions.explanation: Cache entries have a limited lifetime that refreshes on use, so sparse traffic can let an entry lapse between requests.

questions.question: Select the TWO conditions under which prompt caching delivers meaningful savings.

options.A: Each request contains entirely new text with no shared prefix
options.B: A large reference document is resent unchanged across many requests
options.C: A lengthy static system prompt precedes a short varying user message on every call
options.D: Requests are large but each is issued exactly once

questions.explanation: Savings require a substantial prefix that repeats across calls. Content that is unique per request, or large but never reused, cannot produce cache reads.

questions.question: In what order is a request's cacheable prefix built, and why does it matter?

options.A: tools, then system, then messages; a change at one level invalidates the cache for everything after it
options.B: There is no order; any change invalidates only that block
options.C: messages, then system, then tools; only message changes matter
options.D: Alphabetical by field name

questions.explanation: Caching is an exact prefix match. Keep stable content first (frozen tool list, static system prompt) and volatile content after the last cache breakpoint.

questions.question: A team toggles thinking or effort settings on some requests that share a large cached prefix, and cache reads fall. What is happening?

options.A: The cache TTL is reset to zero by streaming
options.B: Changing thinking configuration (or a top-level effort setting) mid-conversation invalidates the cached messages, so the reuse is lost
options.C: Thinking tokens are cached separately and always hit
options.D: Effort only affects output, so caching cannot change

questions.explanation: Settings that change how the model processes the request are part of what a cache entry depends on. Decide thinking/effort per route rather than flipping it per request against a shared prefix.

questions.question: Select the TWO accurate statements about prompt caching limits.

options.A: A request can have at most four cache breakpoints
options.B: Cache entries live forever once written
options.C: A prefix shorter than the model's minimum cacheable length silently does not cache, with no error
options.D: Cache reads cost the same as uncached input

questions.explanation: Up to four breakpoints per request. Minimum cacheable length is model-dependent (roughly 512 to 4,096 tokens), and falling short is silent: the cache usage counters stay at zero. Reads cost about a tenth of base input on most models.

questions.question: Traffic sharing a large prefix arrives in bursts roughly every 20 minutes. Which cache TTL fits, and what does it cost?

options.A: The 5-minute TTL, since it refreshes itself without traffic
options.B: The 1-hour TTL, which is free to write
options.C: The 1-hour TTL, whose writes cost about 2x base input, because the 5-minute entry would expire between bursts
options.D: No caching, since the prefix is shared

questions.explanation: A cache read refreshes the entry's timer at no extra cost. If requests sharing a prefix start less than 5 minutes apart, the default stays warm; longer gaps call for the 1-hour TTL (2x write) or a keep-alive request.

questions.question: A product manager asks for 'an AI assistant that answers questions about customer accounts'. The platform serves many tenant companies and keeps an audit log for regulators. What should happen before choosing an architecture?

options.A: Copy the retrieval design from a neighbouring single-tenant product
options.B: Elicit the unstated constraints first: tenant isolation rules, what must be audited, residency, and failure modes, because a mistake there is silent and costly
options.C: Build a quick prototype and fix tenancy issues as users report them
options.D: Ship behind a feature flag and monitor for problems

questions.explanation: Standing constraints such as multiple tenants and audit obligations predate the request and appear in no description of it. Iteration needs a signal, and a tenancy or authorization defect emits none until it becomes an incident, so these must be elicited before building.

questions.question: Which of these is a testable functional requirement?

options.A: 'The assistant should use the best available model.'
options.B: 'The assistant should be fast and accurate.'
options.C: 'For an order ID the caller does not own, the assistant returns a not-found response and no order details.'
options.D: 'Responses should feel seamless to users.'

questions.explanation: A functional requirement names an observable behaviour someone can mark pass or fail. 'Fast', 'accurate' and 'seamless' are goals until converted into a check; naming a model is a design choice, not a requirement.

questions.question: A team must choose between a hosted agent runtime and self-hosting. A contract states that customer data may only be processed in the EU. How should this constraint be used in the decision?

options.A: As a concern to revisit after launch
options.B: As one weighted factor in a scoring matrix alongside cost and latency
options.C: As something the model provider handles automatically
options.D: As a filter that produces the candidate list; options that cannot satisfy it are eliminated before latency, cost or familiarity are compared

questions.explanation: Regulations, jurisdictions and retention obligations decide which options are admissible. Speed, cost and familiarity only order what survives the rule; they never overturn it.

questions.question: Functional behaviour for a new Claude feature is fully specified and a platform decision is due. Which additional facts must be obtained before deciding?

options.A: Infrastructure requirements: latency measured at the user, peak volume, where data may be processed and stored, and whose credentials act with what audit record
options.B: Which platform the previous project used
options.C: The team's favourite programming language
options.D: The public benchmark ranking of each model

questions.explanation: Infrastructure requirements bound the deployment rather than the behaviour. They are obtained by asking the people who hold them, because each is obvious to its owner and invisible in the functional spec.

questions.question: A teammate proposes reusing another team's authorization approach because 'their system looks just like ours'. What is the right response?

options.A: Reuse it and add monitoring to catch differences
options.B: Check which of that system's assumptions (tenancy, roles, data ownership) actually hold here before reusing it
options.C: Reuse it, since similar shape implies similar requirements
options.D: Reject reuse on principle

questions.explanation: Copying an approach imports its assumptions along with its structure, and an authorization path is where an imported assumption does the most damage.

questions.question: A service has a strict 300 ms latency budget. What does that tell you about which tenant may see which records?

options.A: That only the fastest model may be used
options.B: That authorization can be skipped for cached responses
options.C: Nothing; a performance target implies no correctness or authorization rule, which must be elicited separately
options.D: That caching across tenants is permitted to meet the budget

questions.explanation: Inferring a correctness rule from a performance target is guessing. Latency and data-access rules are separate requirements with separate owners.

questions.question: Why record the source of each constraint (a regulation, a contract clause, a security review) alongside an architecture decision?

options.A: It makes the system run faster
options.B: It removes the need for tests
options.C: It is required for the model to read the decision
options.D: Reviewers who were not present when constraints were gathered can see that the design is a consequence of named constraints, not a habit, and can tell when a constraint changes

questions.explanation: A decision record holds the behaviours, the constraints and where each came from. Without sources, a defensible design looks arbitrary to anyone outside the team and cannot be revisited safely.

questions.question: When is iterating quickly toward a fix (prototype, ship, observe) an appropriate way to discover requirements?

options.A: When the change is reversible and failures are loud, cheap and contained
options.B: Always, since production traffic is the best teacher
options.C: When the system handles multiple tenants' private data
options.D: When an audit trail is legally required

questions.explanation: Monitoring and canaries find constraints by violating them. That is a fair trade when failure is cheap and visible, and a bad one when failure is silent, rare and consequential.

questions.question: Select the TWO statements about inference location and data residency that are accurate for the Claude API.

options.A: Where inference runs and where data is stored are separate settings
options.B: Inference location can only be set once per organisation and never per request
options.C: Residency is always satisfied automatically by choosing a nearby region in the SDK
options.D: A residency requirement that arrives late can force a rebuild, because some placement decisions are fixed when a workspace is created

questions.explanation: Geography is two settings: a per-request inference control (inference_geo, with a workspace default) and a data storage location fixed at workspace creation. Discovering the requirement after launch can therefore cost a migration rather than a config change.

questions.question: A multi-user chat backend 'continues the most recent session' when a request arrives. Users occasionally see another conversation's context. What is wrong?

options.A: The API stores sessions per API key
options.B: The model is leaking memory between users
options.C: Continuing by recency is not identity; in anything serving more than one conversation, the session must be selected by an explicit identifier tied to the user
options.D: Sessions must be continued by timestamp instead

questions.explanation: Continue resolves by recency, resume resolves by identifier, and fork copies a history into a new identifier. Only an identifier lets identity select the session.

questions.question: Agent sessions are resumed on a different worker machine from the one that created them, and resumption fails. Why?

options.A: Resumption requires the same IP address
options.B: The model forgets sessions after an hour
options.C: Sessions can never be resumed
options.D: Session transcripts are stored locally on the machine that created them, so another host can only resume a session if the transcript is made available there, typically by mirroring it to shared storage with a session store

questions.explanation: Session files live on the machine that created them, so a different worker cannot find them. To resume across hosts, attach a session store adapter that mirrors transcripts to shared storage (and resume from a matching working directory), copy the session's .jsonl file to the new host, or skip resume and pass the needed state into a fresh session.

questions.question: Select the TWO statements about starting a fresh conversation that are accurate.

options.A: Ending a session immediately deletes its stored transcript
options.B: An idle timeout covers every case where stale context should be dropped
options.C: A timeout alone is insufficient; defined events (logout, task completion, role change) and the application's own judgement of new intent are also needed
options.D: A rule that depends on the user choosing to start a new chat is not a guarantee

questions.explanation: The clock, events and intent each close a different door into a new conversation. Ending a session stops traffic but does not delete stored transcripts; retention follows its documented or configured period.

questions.question: A session is resumed after a crash. Which of these does NOT come back automatically?

options.A: Launch-time configuration such as an elevated permission mode, which must be passed again
options.B: The conversation history
options.C: The record of earlier tool calls in the transcript
options.D: The model the session used

questions.explanation: Resuming restores the conversation, including earlier tool calls, and normally the model. It does not restore every launch-time setting. A session that was running with bypassPermissions or in plan mode comes back in the default mode, and flags such as --mcp-config, --settings and --add-dir must be passed again, so elevated settings have to be re-supplied on purpose.

questions.question: What does forking a session do?

options.A: Merges two sessions into one
options.B: Deletes the original session
options.C: Resumes whichever session was used most recently
options.D: Copies an existing history into a new session identifier, so a new line of work starts from the same point without altering the original

questions.explanation: Continue picks by recency, resume by identifier, and fork branches a copy under a new identifier.

questions.question: A job sends 10,000 classification calls by launching them all at once. It hits rate-limit errors, and many calls exhaust their retries. What is the best fix?

options.A: Run every call strictly sequentially in one loop
options.B: Use a bounded pool of concurrent workers (or the Batches API if nobody is waiting) so the burst becomes a steady rate within the limit
options.C: Use several API keys to spread the load
options.D: Launch the calls with no delay but add more retries per call

questions.explanation: Unbounded fan-out meets the rate limit as a wall and burns retry budget the queued work needs. Bounded concurrency turns a burst into a rate; volume with no waiting caller is the cue for asynchronous batch submission.

questions.question: After a timeout, a client retried a 'create invoice' call and two invoices were created. What design change prevents this?

options.A: Increase the timeout so retries happen less often
options.B: Add exponential backoff to the retry
options.C: Make the operation idempotent: send a unique key with each unit of work so the receiver recognises a repeat and does not apply it twice
options.D: Stop retrying any request

questions.explanation: Retriability is about the cause; safety is about what already happened. Backoff and timeouts change when a repeat happens, not whether it double-writes. An idempotency key makes the unit of work safe to repeat.

questions.question: A concurrent pipeline sends requests and writes each result back to the record at the same list index. Some results land on the wrong record, with no errors. Why?

options.A: The API reorders requests deliberately to save cost
options.B: List indexes are not thread-safe in any language
options.C: Results are only out of order when streaming is enabled
options.D: Completion order differs from submission order; each request must carry a correlation key that returns with its result, and results must be joined on that key

questions.explanation: Once work overlaps, results arrive with no positional relationship to the request. Joining on position updates the wrong record and raises no error. The same rule applies to batch results and custom_id.

questions.question: Code handling Claude API errors uses an exhaustive switch over every documented error type and throws on anything else. What is the risk?

options.A: The versioning policy reserves the right for error type values to grow, so a new value lands in no branch; branch on known values and keep a safe default
options.B: Error types never change, so there is no risk
options.C: The API rejects clients that use switch statements
options.D: Exhaustive switches are slower than if-else chains

questions.explanation: A contract is what is promised plus what is reserved. Handle the values you know, default the rest, log the request identifier, and never match on message text.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the Claude Messages API as an HTTP interface?

options.A: A WebSocket API that keeps a persistent session per user
options.B: A RESTful JSON API: you POST to /v1/messages with a credential header, an anthropic-version header and a JSON body, and the service keeps no state between calls
options.C: A stateful API that stores each conversation by ID
options.D: A SOAP API requiring XML envelopes

questions.explanation: Each request needs a credential (x-api-key or an Authorization bearer token), anthropic-version and content-type: application/json. Statelessness means continuity is something your code supplies.

questions.question: A service must push live updates to a browser and receive user messages back over the same long-lived connection. Which shape fits?

options.A: Short polling every 500 ms
options.B: A single request and response
options.C: A WebSocket, because both ends send unprompted over one persistent connection
options.D: Server-sent events, which are naturally two-way

questions.explanation: Persistence and two-way messaging are separate properties. SSE (which Claude streaming uses) pushes server-to-client only; polling pins staleness to the interval. Two-way, long-lived exchanges are what WebSockets are for.

questions.question: Select the TWO practices for robust JSON handling of API responses.

options.A: Coerce missing values to an empty string so downstream code never fails
options.B: Read fields by name and ignore unknown fields rather than rejecting the whole object
options.C: Treat an absent field and a field that is null as different statements
options.D: Parse responses positionally, by the order fields appear

questions.explanation: Tolerate additions, keep absent, null and empty distinct, and reject real type mismatches visibly. Coercing a missing value into a present one hides failures.

questions.question: A team must replace a deprecated request parameter whose replacement behaves differently, across 40 call sites, within six months. What is the best plan?

options.A: Change all 40 call sites on the deadline day
options.B: Write a compatibility wrapper that maps the old parameter to the new one
options.C: Leave it until the parameter is removed
options.D: Pin current behaviour in tests, then migrate in small batches whose effects can each be attributed

questions.explanation: A replacement that acts on something different is not a rename. A wrapper keeps the call shape and loses the semantics; a deadline-day migration concentrates every semantic change into one push with no slack.

questions.question: Why should a large refactor and a behaviour change land in separate commits?

options.A: So a later symptom can be attributed to one or the other; mixed together, history cannot tell you which change caused it
options.B: Because Git cannot store both in one commit
options.C: Because refactors must always be reviewed by a different team
options.D: Because behaviour changes must not include tests

questions.explanation: Restructuring changes form and nothing observable; behaviour changes are what break things. Separating them costs one extra commit and keeps the history attributable.

questions.question: Which asynchronous approach keeps a web server responsive while it waits on several Claude calls for a user who is watching?

options.A: Prompt caching, which makes calls concurrent
options.B: Non-blocking async calls, which overlap the waiting so one process can hold many requests in flight
options.C: A sequential loop, which is simpler
options.D: The Message Batches API, which returns faster

questions.explanation: Async concurrency is overlapping waiting, not parallel computation, and responses still arrive at conversational speed. A batch surrenders that speed for a discount, so it does not fit a waiting user.

questions.question: An API response comes back with stop_reason 'end_turn'. What does this tell the calling application?

options.A: The request failed and should be retried
options.B: The output was cut off by the max_tokens ceiling
options.C: The model finished its turn naturally, so the response can be treated as complete
options.D: The model is waiting for a tool result

questions.explanation: end_turn means natural completion. Other values demand other actions: tool_use (run the tool and return a result), max_tokens or model_context_window_exceeded (output is truncated), pause_turn (send the assistant content back to resume), and refusal (a 200 response the model declined; check stop_details and consider a fallback model).

questions.question: A response is unexpectedly cut off mid-sentence with stop_reason 'max_tokens'. What is the most direct fix?

options.A: Lower the temperature parameter
options.B: Increase the max_tokens value for the request (and/or continue generation in a follow-up call)
options.C: Switch to the Batches API
options.D: Add more few-shot examples to the prompt

questions.explanation: 'max_tokens' as a stop reason means the output hit its length ceiling; raising the max_tokens parameter or continuing the generation resolves the truncation.

questions.question: A response returns with a stop reason indicating the token ceiling was reached. What should the application do?

options.A: Recognize the output is incomplete and either raise the ceiling or request a continuation
options.B: Treat the partial output as final and display it
options.C: Retry the identical request, since the result is nondeterministic
options.D: Discard the output and report a server error to the user

questions.explanation: Hitting the ceiling means the output was cut off mid-generation. The fix is a larger budget or an explicit continuation, not treating truncated text as a finished answer.

questions.question: A response's stop reason indicates the model wants to use a tool. What does this signal about the conversation?

options.A: The tool has already run and its output is in the text block
options.B: It has paused awaiting the application to execute the tool and return a result
options.C: The request failed validation and must be resubmitted
options.D: It has ended and no further turns are possible

questions.explanation: That stop reason is a handoff: the model has produced a tool request and is waiting for the application to execute it and supply the result so the exchange can continue.

questions.question: An application configured a stop sequence and now sees responses ending earlier than intended. What is the likely cause?

options.A: Stop sequences are advisory and cannot end generation
options.B: The model ignores stop sequences when tools are defined
options.C: The configured string occurs naturally in the generated content, halting output there
options.D: Stop sequences apply only to the system prompt

questions.explanation: Generation halts at the first occurrence of a configured stop string, so a sequence that appears naturally in normal output will truncate responses unintentionally.

questions.question: Why is branching on the stop reason preferable to inspecting only the text content of a response?

options.A: Different terminations demand different follow-up actions that the text alone does not distinguish
options.B: Text content is unavailable unless streaming is enabled
options.C: The stop reason is the only field that contains the model's answer
options.D: The stop reason guarantees the response is factually correct

questions.explanation: Natural completion, truncation, a stop-sequence halt, and a tool request all require different handling, and the text alone does not reliably distinguish them.

questions.question: A response returns HTTP 200 with stop_reason 'refusal'. How should the application treat it?

options.A: As a network failure to retry immediately with the same model
options.B: As a successful answer and display the content
options.C: As a malformed request needing a code fix
options.D: As a declined response, not a transport error: read stop_details for the category and, where appropriate, retry on a fallback model

questions.explanation: Refusals arrive on a successful 200, so status-code-only error handling misses them. Check stop_reason before reading content, record refusals separately, and use fallbacks where offered.

questions.question: A request using the server-side web search tool returns stop_reason 'pause_turn'. What should the application do?

options.A: Send the assistant content back as-is in the next request so the model can continue the paused turn
options.B: Treat the response as complete
options.C: Return tool_result blocks for the web searches
options.D: Raise max_tokens and resend the original request

questions.explanation: pause_turn means the server-side tool loop hit its iteration limit. Unlike tool_use, there are no results to supply: append the assistant response and continue.

questions.question: When consuming a streamed response, which correctly describes the relationship between the 'message_start' and 'content_block_start' events?

options.A: 'message_start' always arrives after 'content_block_start' regardless of stream order
options.B: Both are part of the ordered sequence of server-sent events that together let the client reconstruct the full message incrementally
options.C: Only one of these two events is ever emitted in a given stream
options.D: These events are unrelated to streaming and only appear in non-streaming responses

questions.explanation: Claude's streaming API emits an ordered sequence of SSE events (message_start, content_block_start/delta/stop, message_delta, message_stop) that the client accumulates to reconstruct the full response.

questions.question: A client renders streamed output but the final text is missing fragments. Which implementation error is most likely?

options.A: Requesting streaming without also raising the token ceiling
options.B: Rendering each delta event in isolation instead of accumulating them in order
options.C: Failing to poll the endpoint frequently enough between events
options.D: Using a single HTTP connection rather than one per event

questions.explanation: Streamed responses arrive as ordered incremental deltas that the client accumulates into the full message; treating each event as a standalone value loses content.

questions.question: Which best characterizes how streaming is requested and delivered?

options.A: The client polls a job identifier until the response is ready
options.B: A separate streaming endpoint returns a WebSocket handle
options.C: The response arrives as a single JSON object with an array of deltas
options.D: A parameter on the ordinary Messages request switches the response to a sequence of server-sent events

questions.explanation: Streaming is a flag on the normal Messages request; the response then arrives as a server-sent event stream rather than one blocking payload.

questions.question: During a long stream, a client sees periodic events carrying no content. How should these be handled?

options.A: Treated as keep-alive traffic and ignored for rendering purposes
options.B: Treated as end-of-message markers
options.C: Treated as errors requiring the stream to be restarted
options.D: Rendered as blank lines to preserve fidelity

questions.explanation: Contentless events keep the connection alive during generation gaps; a robust client ignores unrecognized or empty event types rather than failing on them.

questions.question: An error occurs after a stream has already begun emitting text. How does this surface?

options.A: As an error event within the stream, after content has already been delivered
options.B: As a silent connection close with no indication
options.C: As a non-200 HTTP status on the original request
options.D: It cannot happen; errors only occur before the first event

questions.explanation: The HTTP response has already succeeded by then, so mid-stream failures arrive as an error event inside the stream, which clients must handle alongside content events.

questions.question: Which requirement most strongly favors streaming over a single blocking response?

options.A: A pipeline that needs the complete response before any downstream step
options.B: A request that must be retried automatically on failure
options.C: A conversational UI where users should see output begin within a moment
options.D: A nightly job writing results to a database with no user waiting

questions.explanation: Streaming reduces perceived latency where a human is watching output appear. Batch and pipeline work that needs the whole response first gains nothing from it.

questions.question: While consuming a stream, where does the final stop_reason arrive?

options.A: In the first message_start event
options.B: In the message_delta event near the end of the stream; it is null in message_start
options.C: In an HTTP response header
options.D: It is never available when streaming

questions.explanation: message_start carries the message shell, content blocks stream via start/delta/stop events, then message_delta carries stop_reason and final usage, followed by message_stop.

questions.question: A retail chatbot must return both a natural-language explanation and a machine-readable result that a program consumes, in one turn. What is the most robust approach?

options.A: Make two separate, uncoordinated API calls and hope the outputs match
options.B: Structured output is impossible with the Claude API
options.C: Define a JSON schema with an explanation field and the result fields, and request it through structured outputs (output_config.format), validating values on receipt
options.D: Ask for prose and extract the values with a regular expression

questions.explanation: Structured outputs compile your JSON schema into a grammar that constrains generation, so the response always parses. An explanation can simply be a string field in the schema. You still validate values on receipt, because a schema guarantees shape, not correctness.

questions.question: A service needs JSON conforming to a fixed schema and occasionally receives prose wrapped around the object. Which combination is the most robust fix?

options.A: Constrain generation with structured outputs (a JSON schema in output_config.format, or strict: true on a tool), and keep validating values on receipt
options.B: Lower temperature to zero, which guarantees schema conformance
options.C: Switch to a larger model and accept the output unvalidated
options.D: Raise the token ceiling and retry until prose stops appearing

questions.explanation: Structured outputs remove the malformed-output failure class by constraining sampling to the schema. Validation on receipt stays, because refusals and max_tokens truncation still return without usable structure, and SDKs strip constraints (such as ranges) the grammar cannot express. Sampling settings never guarantee shape, and non-default temperature is rejected on Claude 4.7 and later.

questions.question: Why is tool use a practical mechanism for obtaining structured data even when no external action is performed?

options.A: Tool calls bypass the model's token budget
options.B: Tool results are validated server-side before being returned
options.C: Tool inputs are schema-defined, so the model's output is shaped by that schema
options.D: Tool definitions are cached automatically and cost nothing

questions.explanation: A tool definition carries an input schema, so a tool call yields schema-shaped arguments, and strict: true on the tool guarantees they validate. For a fixed-shape final response, the dedicated feature is now structured outputs (output_config.format).

questions.question: An extraction service must handle documents where a required field is genuinely absent. What schema design best prevents fabricated values?

options.A: Make every field required so the model always returns something
options.B: Allow an explicit null or not-found value for the field and instruct the model to use it
options.C: Omit the field from the schema entirely
options.D: Retry with a higher temperature until a plausible value appears

questions.explanation: Giving the model a legitimate way to report absence removes the pressure to invent a value. Forcing every field to be populated actively encourages fabrication.

questions.question: Select the TWO ways a structured-outputs request can still return without usable structured data.

options.A: The model refuses (stop_reason 'refusal')
options.B: The JSON violates the declared schema's types
options.C: The response contains a property not declared in the schema
options.D: Generation is cut off at max_tokens

questions.explanation: Structured outputs compile the schema into a grammar, so type violations cannot be produced. The documented escapes are refusals and truncation, which is why you check stop_reason before parsing. Enum casing and unsupported constraints are other reasons to validate on receipt.

questions.question: A Claude-powered system has just gone live. Which description best fits the phase it has entered?

options.A: A one-time launch review
options.B: An ongoing operate-and-maintain phase with no completion date: it must be watched, answered for and evolved until it is switched off
options.C: The end of the model's lifecycle
options.D: A finished project that can now be handed off and forgotten

questions.explanation: Development finishes; operation does not. Activities like launch reviews and retrospectives are finite events inside this open-ended phase.

questions.question: A team tracks failures only by HTTP error rate. Usable responses are falling while the dashboard stays flat. What is the most likely blind spot?

options.A: The dashboard refresh interval is too long
options.B: The API is hiding its 5xx errors
options.C: Refusals and other unusable 200 responses (truncations, malformed output) are not counted as failures
options.D: Streaming responses are never counted

questions.explanation: A refusal arrives as a successful response with stop_reason 'refusal', and truncation as 'max_tokens'. A failure metric built on transport errors reads flat while usable output declines, so track these outcomes separately.

questions.question: Which three quantities should a Claude-backed service emit from its first day in production?

options.A: Lines of code, commit count and team size
options.B: Only the average response length
options.C: Only total monthly spend from the invoice
options.D: Cost per call, latency, and failures (including refusals and truncations)

questions.explanation: Without cost, latency and failure telemetry, nobody can say what the system costs or how often it fails usefully. Treat in-app cost figures as an approximation to trend; billing comes from the provider.

questions.question: Anthropic announces that the model your production system uses will retire on a stated date. What is the correct response?

options.A: Schedule the migration as planned work with an owner and a date inside the notice window, scored against the current baseline before switching
options.B: Wait until the retirement date and switch then
options.C: Switch immediately to the newest model without evaluation
options.D: Ignore it; deprecated models keep working indefinitely

questions.explanation: Anthropic gives at least 60 days' notice before retiring a publicly released model, and requests to retired models fail. Deferring turns a planned migration into an outage; switching without an eval means you cannot tell what the swap cost.

questions.question: Your system runs Claude on Amazon Bedrock. Whose retirement schedule applies to the model you use there?

options.A: None; models on cloud platforms never retire
options.B: Bedrock's own published schedule, since partner-operated platforms set their own retirement dates
options.C: Whichever date is later
