options.D: Only Anthropic's first-party schedule

questions.explanation: Anthropic's deprecation dates apply to Anthropic-operated platforms. Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud set their own schedules, so the same model can have a different lifecycle status depending on where it runs.

questions.question: A new prompt version is ready. What should happen before it receives production traffic?

options.A: Promote it to half the users and ask them which they prefer
options.B: Promote it if the new text reads better to the author
options.C: Score it against the current baseline on the evaluation set and promote only if it clears the gate
options.D: Promote it and watch production metrics for differences

questions.explanation: A gate is real only if it can refuse, and it refuses against a named artifact such as an eval score versus baseline. Promoting first and observing production discovers regressions by shipping them.

questions.question: An on-call engineer discovers in production that users routinely paste documents in a format the requirements never mentioned. Where should this finding go?

options.A: Into the incident log only
options.B: Into a private note for the next on-call shift
options.C: Nowhere; production behaviour is not a requirement
options.D: Back into the requirements and evaluation set as a gated change, so the new input class is specified and tested

questions.explanation: Iteration means a production finding reaches the requirement it contradicts and re-enters development through a gate. Left in an incident record, it is knowledge held by one person.

questions.question: A team wants to skip the evaluation gate to hit a launch date. What is the strongest argument against it?

options.A: Skipping a gate raises no error: the system works on the day but cannot be reasoned about later, so name what the gate would have refused before agreeing
options.B: Evaluation gates make the model more accurate
options.C: The API will reject requests from untested prompts
options.D: Gates are legally required for all AI systems

questions.explanation: Schedule arguments always sound stronger than an absent signal. Asking what the gate would have caught makes the trade explicit.

questions.question: An application defines its own custom tool named 'get_weather' (name, description and input_schema) in its API request. Which of the following correctly describes what happens next?

options.A: Claude may respond with a request to call 'get_weather' (including generated input), but the application is responsible for actually executing it and returning the result in a follow-up message
options.B: Claude executes 'get_weather' directly against the live backend itself
options.C: Tool definitions are purely documentation and never affect model behavior
options.D: 'get_weather' is executed automatically by Anthropic's servers with no application involvement

questions.explanation: For a custom (client) tool, Claude does not execute anything itself. It returns a tool_use block with stop_reason 'tool_use', and the calling application runs the tool and sends the output back in a tool_result block in the next user message. Only Anthropic-provided server tools, such as web search, run on Anthropic's infrastructure.

questions.question: An application defines its own custom tool named 'lookup_inventory' (name, description and input_schema) in its API request. Which of the following correctly describes what happens next?

options.A: Claude may respond with a request to call 'lookup_inventory' (including generated input), but the application is responsible for actually executing it and returning the result in a follow-up message
options.B: 'lookup_inventory' is executed automatically by Anthropic's servers with no application involvement
options.C: Tool definitions are purely documentation and never affect model behavior
options.D: Claude executes 'lookup_inventory' directly against the live backend itself

questions.explanation: For a custom (client) tool, Claude does not execute anything itself. It returns a tool_use block with stop_reason 'tool_use', and the calling application runs the tool and sends the output back in a tool_result block in the next user message. Only Anthropic-provided server tools, such as web search, run on Anthropic's infrastructure.

questions.question: An application defines a tool named 'calculate_shipping' in its API request. Which of the following correctly describes what happens next?

options.A: Tool definitions are purely documentation and never affect model behavior
options.B: 'calculate_shipping' is executed automatically by Anthropic's servers with no application involvement
options.C: Claude executes 'calculate_shipping' directly against the live backend itself
options.D: Claude may respond with a request to call 'calculate_shipping' (including generated input), but the application is responsible for actually executing it and returning the result in a follow-up message

questions.explanation: 'calculate_shipping' is a user-defined (client) tool, so Claude does not execute it: Claude returns a tool_use block with the tool name and generated input, and the calling application executes the tool and sends the result back as a tool_result content block in a user message. Only Anthropic-provided server tools, such as web search or code execution, run on Anthropic's infrastructure.

questions.question: Regarding the tool 'get_weather' defined in an API request, select the TWO true statements.

options.A: Claude decides whether and when to call the tool based on the conversation and the tool's description/schema
options.B: A single API request can only ever define one tool
options.C: The application must execute the tool call and return its result for the conversation to continue meaningfully
options.D: Tool results must be sent back as a new 'system' role message

questions.explanation: Claude autonomously decides when a defined tool is relevant (A); multiple tools can be defined per request (so B is false); execution and returning results is the application's job (C); tool results go back as a 'user' message with a tool_result content block, not a system message (so D is false).

questions.question: A tool executes but raises an exception. How should this be reported back to the model?

options.A: Return a successful result containing an empty value
options.B: Return a tool result flagged as an error, describing what went wrong
options.C: Abort the conversation and start a new one
options.D: Omit the result and send only a user message describing the problem

questions.explanation: Returning a result marked as an error, with a description, lets the model adapt — retry with different arguments, choose another tool, or explain the failure. Silently returning empty success invites wrong conclusions.

questions.question: A response contains two tool-use blocks. What must the next request include?

options.A: No results, since parallel calls are executed server-side
options.B: A result for the first call only, deferring the second
options.C: A single merged result covering both calls under one identifier
options.D: A tool_result for each call, each echoing its tool_use_id, together in the next user message

questions.explanation: Every tool_use block must be answered by its own tool_result (matched by tool_use_id) before the conversation can continue. Return them together in one user message; splitting them across messages works against parallel tool use.

questions.question: What makes a tool description important to the quality of tool use?

options.A: It is shown to end users in the interface
options.B: It is used only for API documentation and has no runtime effect
options.C: It determines the tool's execution timeout
options.D: It is the primary basis on which the model decides whether and how to call the tool

questions.explanation: The description and parameter schema are the model's only information about a tool's purpose and correct use, so vague descriptions are a leading cause of wrong or missing calls.

questions.question: Select the TWO accurate statements about defining tools on a request.

options.A: The API executes a defined tool automatically and returns its output
options.B: Several tools may be defined on a single request and the model chooses among them
options.C: Only one tool definition is permitted per request
options.D: The model generates the tool's arguments but the application performs the execution

questions.explanation: Multiple tools can be offered and the model selects; it produces the arguments while the caller executes. The API never runs a tool itself, and there is no single-tool limit.

questions.question: In a tool result turn, a developer adds a text block after the tool_result blocks saying 'Here is the result'. Over time responses come back empty with stop_reason 'end_turn'. What is the likely cause?

options.A: Adding text right after tool results teaches the model to expect user input after every tool use; send only the tool_result blocks
options.B: The API strips text after tool results
options.C: Empty responses always mean a rate limit
options.D: The tool_use_id was wrong

questions.explanation: A tool-result turn should carry the tool_result blocks for the calls it answers. Extra text there is a documented cause of empty end_turn responses.

questions.question: A team wants to integrate Claude into a Python codebase. Which statement is accurate?

options.A: Claude can only be accessed through a graphical interface, never programmatically
options.B: Raw HTTP calls to the API are blocked and require an SDK
options.C: Only Python is capable of calling the Claude API
options.D: Official client SDKs exist for common languages, and for any language the underlying Messages API can be called directly over HTTP

questions.explanation: Anthropic provides official SDKs for common languages, and since the API is a standard HTTP/JSON interface, any language capable of making HTTP requests can integrate directly.

questions.question: A single user turn must carry an instruction, a PDF contract and two screenshots. How is this expressed in a Messages API request?

options.A: As four separate API calls, one per item, whose answers the application merges
options.B: As one user message whose content is a list of typed blocks: document, image, image, and text
options.C: By base64-encoding everything into the system prompt
options.D: Through the legacy Text Completions endpoint, which accepts attachments

questions.explanation: Message content is a list of typed content blocks, so text, images and documents travel together through the one Messages endpoint. Anthropic recommends placing long documents and images before the instruction text.

questions.question: A team wants to integrate Claude from a language with no official SDK. What is the most direct path?

options.A: Call the HTTP/JSON endpoints directly from that language
options.B: Rewrite the service in a language that has an official SDK
options.C: Route calls through a browser automation harness
options.D: Wait for an official SDK, since direct HTTP access is not supported

questions.explanation: The API is a standard HTTP/JSON interface, so any language capable of issuing HTTP requests can integrate without an SDK.

questions.question: Where should an API key live in a production deployment?

options.A: In the client-side bundle so the browser can call the API directly and reduce hops
options.B: Committed to the repository so every environment stays in sync
options.C: In server-side configuration or a secret manager, with requests proxied through your backend
options.D: Embedded in the mobile binary, obfuscated

questions.explanation: Keys must stay server-side in configuration or a secret store, with the application proxying calls; anything shipped to a client is retrievable by users.

questions.question: Which headers are required on a raw HTTP call to the Messages API?

options.A: A credential (x-api-key or an Authorization bearer token), anthropic-version, and content-type: application/json
options.B: No headers; everything goes in the body
options.C: Only the API key
options.D: anthropic-model and accept-language

questions.explanation: The official SDKs send these automatically. A missing or wrong header fails identically on every attempt, which is how you recognise an integration-seam failure.

questions.question: A team starts a new Python integration and proposes wrapping a generic HTTP library because 'it's only three headers'. What is the main argument for the official SDK?

options.A: The SDK makes tokens cheaper
options.B: It maintains the boilerplate for you: typed exceptions, a default retry policy, timeouts and keep-alive, pagination, request IDs, and tracking API changes
options.C: The SDK reaches a smarter model than raw HTTP
options.D: Raw HTTP calls are blocked

questions.explanation: The SDK and a hand-written call reach the same endpoint and model. What changes is who maintains the parts as the API moves; a hand-rolled client becomes a private fork.

questions.question: Why is calling Claude through an OpenAI-compatible shim a weak default for a new Claude-only application?

options.A: Shims are illegal under the API terms
options.B: The shim is always more expensive per token
options.C: Compatibility layers are not general-purpose Messages API clients; they add a layer to debug and can hide Claude-specific features, for a provider switch nobody scheduled
options.D: Shims cannot send text

questions.explanation: Portability is a real requirement only when it is real. For a Claude-only project, the native SDK gives full feature access without a translation layer.

questions.question: How does the API know which model to use for a request?

options.A: A separate endpoint per model
options.B: The model is chosen automatically from the prompt
options.C: The model is fixed per API key
options.D: The required model field in the JSON body, alongside max_tokens and messages

questions.explanation: Every Messages request names a model, a max_tokens ceiling, and a messages list; standing instructions go in the top-level system field. On some cloud platforms the model moves into the URL, but the message shape is unchanged.

questions.question: A workload is not latency-sensitive and can tolerate being processed within a multi-hour window. Which combination of optimizations would most reduce cost?

options.A: Use synchronous real-time calls to guarantee lowest cost
options.B: Use only the largest model with no caching
options.C: Use the Message Batches API and apply prompt caching where inputs share static content
options.D: Disable caching to simplify the architecture

questions.explanation: Combining Batches API discounts with prompt caching for shared static content stacks cost savings for delay-tolerant, high-repetition workloads.

questions.question: A customer-facing chatbot must minimize cost while keeping answer quality acceptable. Which strategy fits best?

options.A: Route all chat traffic through the Batches API for the 50% discount
options.B: Always use the most capable tier so quality can never be questioned
options.C: Pick the cheapest tier that clears the quality bar on an eval of real conversations, and cache the static system prompt
options.D: Disable all monitoring to reduce overhead

questions.explanation: A user is waiting, so batch is unavailable. The defensible lever is evidence: the cheapest tier (or effort level) that passes an eval of representative traffic, plus caching the stable prefix so repeated system-prompt tokens bill at the read rate.

questions.question: A high-volume triage classifier runs as an overnight job, and minimizing per-request cost is the top priority. Which configuration fits best?

options.A: A light tier at low effort with a short constrained output, submitted through the Batches API
options.B: The most capable tier at maximum effort, called synchronously
options.C: Streaming responses, so tokens are cheaper
options.D: Always the same model and settings as every other workload

questions.explanation: Simple classification rarely needs a large model or deep thinking, a short label keeps output tokens low, and an unattended overnight run qualifies for the batch discount. Streaming changes delivery, not price.

questions.question: A triage classifier sits in a user's request path, and minimizing response latency is the top priority. Which configuration fits best?

options.A: Submit each request through the Batches API
options.B: A lighter tier at low effort, a short output, and a cached static prefix
options.C: The most capable tier at maximum effort, to avoid retries
options.D: A larger max_tokens value so the response is never truncated

questions.explanation: Latency falls with a lighter model, less thinking, fewer output tokens, and a cached prefix (which shortens time to first token). Batch is asynchronous and unsuitable when a request is waiting; max_tokens is a ceiling, not a speed control.

questions.question: A triage workload's top priority is reasoning quality on ambiguous, high-stakes inputs, with relaxed cost limits. Which configuration fits best?

options.A: A more capable tier and/or higher effort, confirmed by an eval on the hardest representative cases
options.B: The cheapest tier, compensated by a longer system prompt
options.C: A very low max_tokens value to keep answers focused
options.D: Raising temperature to explore more interpretations

questions.explanation: When quality on hard cases dominates, capability (tier) and deliberation (effort) are the levers, and an eval on the hardest slice is what shows they paid off. Sampling settings do not add reasoning, and on Claude 4.7 and later non-default temperature is rejected.

questions.question: A nightly job re-scores 200,000 archived documents. Cost matters; completion by morning is sufficient. Which configuration fits best?

options.A: Synchronous calls with streaming enabled
options.B: Synchronous calls with extended thinking enabled for accuracy
options.C: Synchronous calls at maximum concurrency
options.D: Batch submission, accepting asynchronous turnaround for the reduced rate

questions.explanation: High volume with a tolerant deadline is exactly the batch profile: the discount applies and nothing is waiting on the result.

questions.question: A team proposes routing an interactive support chat through batch processing to halve costs. What is the decisive objection?

options.A: Batch requests are billed at a premium for conversational input
options.B: Batch results cannot be parsed programmatically
options.C: Batch processing does not support system prompts
options.D: Batch turnaround is asynchronous and unsuitable for a user waiting on a reply

questions.explanation: The discount is compensation for relaxed turnaround. A live conversation cannot absorb asynchronous processing, so the saving is unavailable at any acceptable user experience.

questions.question: Select the TWO statements that correctly describe the batch/synchronous tradeoff.

options.A: Batch reduces per-request cost in exchange for relaxed completion timing
options.B: Synchronous requests are the right choice whenever a human is waiting on the output
options.C: Batch improves per-request latency compared with synchronous calls
options.D: Batch and synchronous requests are priced identically

questions.explanation: Batch trades timing for cost and suits unattended work; synchronous suits interactive use. It does not improve latency, and the two are not priced alike.

questions.question: A pipeline is partly interactive and partly bulk backfill. What is the most cost-effective architecture?

options.A: Route everything synchronously for operational simplicity
options.B: Route everything through batch and add a spinner to the interactive path
options.C: Split the workload, sending the interactive path synchronously and the backfill through batch
options.D: Alternate between the two modes on a fixed schedule

questions.explanation: Mode should follow each path's latency requirement. Splitting captures the discount where deadlines are loose without degrading the interactive experience.

questions.question: Your application repeats roughly 10% of its input tokens (e.g., shared instructions/context) across many requests. Which optimization most directly reduces cost here?

options.A: Increasing max_tokens
options.B: Adding more tools to the request
options.C: Switching all requests to streaming
options.D: Prompt caching for the repeated portion of the input

questions.explanation: Prompt caching specifically targets repeated static content, cutting cost and latency for the cached portion on subsequent calls.

questions.question: An application's spend is dominated by a 30,000-token reference manual resent with every request. Which lever addresses this most directly?

options.A: Cache the manual as a stable prefix so repeat requests read it cheaply
options.B: Raise the output token ceiling
options.C: Move to a more capable model tier
options.D: Enable streaming to spread cost over time

questions.explanation: A large unchanging prefix resent on every call is the textbook caching case. Neither the ceiling, the tier, nor streaming affects the repeated input cost.

questions.question: Which sequence reflects a sound cost-optimization process?

options.A: Measure where tokens are actually spent, then apply the lever matching the dominant cost
options.B: Disable logging and monitoring to cut overhead
options.C: Reduce the token ceiling until responses fit the budget
options.D: Adopt the cheapest tier immediately and accept whatever quality results

questions.explanation: Optimization starts with measurement: repeated input calls for caching, verbose output for length control, over-provisioned reasoning for a cheaper tier. Guessing at levers wastes effort.

questions.question: Why are input and output tokens considered separately when modeling cost?

options.A: Only output tokens count toward the context window
options.B: Output tokens are free below a threshold
options.C: Input tokens are not billed when a system prompt is present
options.D: They are billed at different rates, so the dominant direction determines the right lever

questions.explanation: Because the two directions are priced differently, an input-heavy workload and an output-heavy one call for different remedies — caching and trimming context versus constraining response length.

questions.question: A tiered routing design sends simple requests to a cheap model and escalates hard ones. What is the main risk to manage?

options.A: Cheaper tiers cannot accept system prompts
options.B: Misclassification, where hard requests are answered poorly by the cheap tier
options.C: Escalation doubles the context window requirement
options.D: Routing is not permitted within a single application

questions.explanation: The saving depends on the router's accuracy. A weak classifier sends difficult work to an under-powered tier, so the routing decision itself needs evaluation.

questions.question: Select the TWO changes that reduce cost without altering the model tier.

options.A: Caching a large static instruction block reused across requests
options.B: Constraining response length where verbose output adds no value
options.C: Setting effort to max on every request regardless of task difficulty
options.D: Resending the full conversation history on every turn regardless of relevance

questions.explanation: Caching stable input and trimming unnecessary output both cut spend at a fixed tier. Running every request at maximum effort removes constraints on token spending, and resending irrelevant history grows input tokens on every turn; both increase cost.

questions.question: A summarization endpoint returns responses far longer than the UI displays. What is the most direct saving?

options.A: Switch to batch processing
options.B: Constrain the requested length so generation stops near what is actually rendered
options.C: Cache the output for reuse
options.D: Increase the token ceiling to avoid truncation retries

questions.explanation: Paying to generate text the interface discards is pure waste; bounding requested length aligns generation with what is consumed. Caching applies to repeated input, not fresh summaries.

questions.question: Before launch, a team needs a monthly cost projection. Which quantities are required?

options.A: Request volume, input tokens per request, output tokens per request, the per-token rates for the chosen model, and the expected share of input served from cache
options.B: Only the number of users
options.C: A per-request figure copied from another product
options.D: Only the per-token input price

questions.explanation: All five are knowable before launch. The token counting endpoint returns input token counts for free, without running inference.

questions.question: Spend is rising and nobody can say which feature drives it. What is the first step?

options.A: Move every feature to the cheapest model
options.B: Instrument token usage per call by feature (tokens in, tokens out, cache reads), then target the dominant cost
options.C: Accept the growth as unavoidable
options.D: Cut max_tokens across every feature

questions.explanation: Attribution precedes optimisation. Every remedy without it is across-the-board and damages features that never drove spend.

questions.question: In a long conversation, cost per exchange climbs steadily even though each user message is short. Which lever addresses this without losing needed history?

options.A: Truncate to the last turn
options.B: Summarise every single turn into one sentence
options.C: Cache the stable prefix (system prompt and earlier turns) so resent history bills at the cache-read rate
options.D: Lower max_tokens

questions.explanation: Because every turn resends the whole history, cost grows roughly with the square of turn count. Caching reuses the prefix instead of deleting context the conversation still needs.

questions.question: To cap spend, a team lowers max_tokens on an agent's requests. Hard tasks now fail partway, and spend barely falls. Why?

options.A: Lower max_tokens always increases price per token
options.B: max_tokens only affects streaming
options.C: The model ignores max_tokens
options.D: max_tokens is invisible to the model and truncates work it has already paid for; a budget the model can see (such as a task budget) paces the work, with a hard limit behind it

questions.explanation: Cutting the ceiling discards the turn that needed the room and still bills its tokens. Spend control that changes behaviour must be something the model can see.

questions.question: Which three settings are independent, and are often confused as one 'quality dial'?

options.A: Model choice (capability tier), thinking (whether and how the model reasons first), and effort (how many tokens it spends)
options.B: Streaming, batching and caching
options.C: Temperature, top_p and top_k
options.D: max_tokens, stop sequences and system prompt length

questions.explanation: A larger model buys capability; thinking and effort buy deliberation on the same model. Fast mode is separate again: a speed setting at premium pricing on supported models.

questions.question: Output quality is already acceptable, but responses from a supported Opus model are too slow for an interactive feature, and budget allows a premium. Which option changes speed without changing what the model produces?

options.A: Submit through the Batches API
options.B: Fast mode, which serves the same model at higher output tokens per second at premium pricing
options.C: Raise effort to maximum
options.D: Switch to a smaller tier

questions.explanation: Fast mode runs the same model with a faster inference configuration at premium pricing. It raises output tokens per second (not time to first token) and does not change the model's intelligence or capabilities. A smaller tier changes the output, and batch processing is asynchronous. Fast mode is a research preview that requires access, is limited to specific Opus models on the Claude API, and is not available with the Batch API.

questions.question: Which workloads typically repay a higher effort setting?

options.A: High-volume chit-chat where latency matters most
options.B: Simple classification
options.C: Coding and long-horizon agentic work
options.D: Echoing or reformatting a string

questions.explanation: Effort trades thoroughness for tokens. Coding and agentic tasks respond strongly; chat and classification often do well at low effort. Tune per route on measured results.

questions.question: An integration built for an older model sends thinking: {type: 'enabled', budget_tokens: 8000}. It now targets Claude Opus 5.5. What happens and what is the fix?

options.A: It works unchanged with an 8,000-token reasoning budget
options.B: The budget is silently converted to max_tokens
options.C: Thinking is disabled and the request succeeds
options.D: The request is rejected with a 400; use adaptive thinking (or omit the parameter) and control depth with output_config.effort

questions.explanation: Fixed thinking budgets are deprecated on the 4.6 models and removed on newer ones. On Opus 5.5 thinking is always on and effort is the control; its default effort is medium, so set it explicitly.

questions.question: On current models the default thinking display is 'omitted', so thinking blocks arrive with empty text. What does that mean for cost?

options.A: Nothing changes: thinking still happens and is billed; display controls only visibility
options.B: Thinking is skipped when its display is omitted
options.C: Omitted thinking halves output cost
options.D: Omitted thinking is free

questions.explanation: If you stream reasoning to users, the default looks like a pause before output, so request a summarized display. Either way, the tokens are billed.

questions.question: Before building a multi-model cascade to cut costs, what simpler alternative should be measured first?

options.A: Running every request twice and picking one
options.B: The most capable model at a lower effort setting on the same tasks
options.C: Using the oldest available model
options.D: Disabling all caching

questions.explanation: Lower effort on a newer model often matches higher effort on older models, and one model keeps one cache namespace, whereas a cascade forfeits cache reuse across models.

questions.question: An application receives an HTTP 400 (invalid_request_error) from the Claude API. What is the correct handling strategy?

options.A: Treat it as a problem with the request itself (format, content, or a limit you set), fix the request, and do not retry it unchanged
options.B: Immediately stop using the API entirely and switch providers
options.C: Resend the identical request in a tight loop until it succeeds
options.D: Back off exponentially and retry the same request, since all errors are transient

questions.explanation: A 400 is deterministic: the same bytes fail the same way on every attempt, so retrying with backoff only pays repeatedly for the same answer. Note it is a catch-all for 4xx conditions without their own code, and a spend limit you set on an organization or workspace also returns a 400, so it is not always proof of a malformed body.

questions.question: An application receives an HTTP 401 (authentication_error) from the Claude API. What is the correct handling strategy?

options.A: Retry with exponential backoff, since authentication failures clear on their own
options.B: Treat all non-200 responses identically regardless of code
options.C: Check the credential: the API key is missing, malformed, revoked or expired, and retrying will not change the outcome
options.D: Increase max_tokens so the request is accepted

questions.explanation: A 401 means the credential is bad. It fails identically on every attempt, so the fix is a valid key (or a refreshed token), not a retry. Compare 403, where the key is valid but lacks permission for the resource.

questions.question: An application receives an HTTP 429 (rate_limit_error) from the Claude API. What is the correct handling strategy?

options.A: Treat all non-200 responses identically regardless of code
options.B: Rotate across several API keys to bypass the limit
options.C: Back off and retry with increasing delays, honoring the retry-after header when present, and cap the number of attempts
options.D: Resend the identical request immediately in a tight loop

questions.explanation: A 429 is usually transient, so bounded retries with exponential backoff that honor retry-after are correct. Two gotchas: the official SDKs already retry 429s twice by default, so wrapping them in your own loop multiplies attempts; and a 429 caused by a usage tier's monthly spend cap carries no retry-after and keeps failing until access resumes.

questions.question: An application receives an HTTP 500 (api_error) from the Claude API. What is the correct handling strategy?

options.A: Immediately stop using the API entirely and switch providers
options.B: Treat it as an unexpected server-side fault: retry with exponential backoff, and if it persists, contact support quoting the request-id
options.C: Rewrite the request body, since a 500 always means the payload is malformed
options.D: Resend the identical request in a tight loop with no delay

questions.explanation: A 500 is an internal error on Anthropic's side. The documented handling is to retry with exponential backoff and, if it persists, contact support with the request-id from the response, which is the only identifier that names a single call.

questions.question: An application receives an HTTP 529 (overloaded_error) from the Claude API. What is the correct handling strategy?

options.A: Treat it as temporary service-wide overload: back off and retry with exponential backoff and a cap on attempts
options.B: Immediately stop using the API entirely and switch providers
options.C: Fix the request body, since a 529 means the request was malformed
options.D: Treat all non-200 responses identically regardless of code

questions.explanation: A 529 reports that the API is temporarily overloaded across users. It is transient, so bounded backoff-and-retry is correct; nothing about your request needs fixing.

questions.question: A client is being rate limited. Which retry behavior is most appropriate?

options.A: Switch to a different model on every retry attempt
options.B: Fail the user's request permanently on the first rate-limit response
options.C: Back off with increasing delays and jitter, honoring any retry-after guidance in the response
options.D: Retry immediately in a tight loop until a request succeeds

questions.explanation: Exponential backoff with jitter, respecting retry-after guidance, drains the queue without amplifying congestion. Tight retry loops make the limit worse.

questions.question: Select the TWO status codes for which retrying the identical request is a reasonable strategy.
questions.explanation: Rate limiting (429) and temporary overload (529) are transient, so the same request may succeed later, and so may a 500. A malformed request (400) and an authentication failure (401) fail identically on every attempt and need the request or the credential fixed.

questions.question: A team wraps the official SDK's calls in their own retry loop of three attempts. Under load, the service sees far more traffic than expected. Why?

options.A: SDKs never retry, so the custom loop is required
options.B: The SDK already retries transient failures (twice by default with backoff), so the nested loops multiply attempts; configure the SDK's max_retries instead of wrapping it
options.C: The SDK's retries cannot be changed or disabled
options.D: The SDK retries only connection errors, never 429s

questions.explanation: The client libraries retry connection errors, 408, 409, 429 and 5xx with exponential backoff, honouring retry-after. Three outer attempts around three inner ones is up to nine requests against a service that asked for a pause.

questions.question: A batch job retries a 429 indefinitely. The 429 has no retry-after header and never clears. What is likely happening?

options.A: A bug in the SDK
options.B: A malformed request body
options.C: The organisation hit its usage tier's monthly spend cap; that 429 keeps failing until access resumes, so unbounded retries turn a billing problem into an outage
options.D: A temporary traffic spike that will clear within seconds

questions.explanation: Not every 429 is transient. Always bound retries and alert when a 429 persists, especially one without retry-after.

questions.question: Which status code means the API key is valid but not permitted to use the requested resource?

options.A: 404 not_found_error
options.B: 429 rate_limit_error
options.C: 401 authentication_error
options.D: 403 permission_error

questions.explanation: 401 means the key itself is bad, 402 is a billing problem, 403 is a valid key lacking permission (for example workspace access). None of them succeed on retry.

questions.question: A request with several large images and PDFs fails with 413 request_too_large. What is the fix?

options.A: Reduce the request size (or use the Files API to reference files), since the Messages API rejects requests over 32 MB; retrying cannot help
options.B: Lower the temperature
options.C: Retry with exponential backoff
options.D: Switch to a model with a larger context window

questions.explanation: 413 is deterministic: the request exceeds the endpoint's byte limit (32 MB for Messages, larger for Batches and Files). It is rejected before reaching the model.

questions.question: Which error-handling style does Anthropic recommend in the official SDKs?

options.A: Ignore exceptions; the SDK retries everything forever
options.B: Catch the SDK's typed exception classes, most specific first (for example not-found, then rate-limit, then generic API status errors), rather than matching message text
options.C: Catch every exception with one broad handler and retry it
options.D: Parse the English error message for keywords

questions.explanation: A single broad catch loses the distinction between retryable (429, 5xx, connection) and non-retryable (400, 404) failures. Message wording is not part of the contract; exception types are.

questions.question: What should an application log when an API call fails so that support can investigate that exact call?

options.A: The local machine's hostname
options.B: Only the HTTP status code
options.C: The request-id returned on every response (also in error bodies)
options.D: The full API key

questions.explanation: The request-id is the only identifier that names a single call. Never log the API key.

questions.question: A non-streaming request with a very large max_tokens repeatedly fails with a timeout on some networks. What is the recommended approach?

options.A: Retry the same non-streaming request in a tight loop
options.B: Lower the temperature
options.C: Split the system prompt across two requests
options.D: Use streaming (the SDK can still assemble the final message) or the Batches API for long generations

questions.explanation: Long non-streaming requests risk idle-connection drops and the SDK's 10-minute expectation. Streaming keeps data flowing; batches let you poll instead of holding a connection.

questions.question: A teammate reports that the same request, sent twice byte-for-byte, returned differently worded answers, and wants to open a bug. What is the right response?

options.A: Pin the model version, which makes outputs identical
options.B: Explain that tokens are sampled, so identical inputs can produce different outputs (even at temperature 0), and make the application tolerant: validate, retry on failure, or constrain the output shape
options.C: Agree it is a bug in request construction and investigate the HTTP client
options.D: Explain that it is expected and close the ticket with no further action

questions.explanation: Run-to-run variation is a property of generation, not a defect. The complete answer names the mechanism and then says what the application does about it; stopping at 'that is expected' ships nothing.

questions.question: A contract is too long to fit in one request, and references in section 9 must resolve against definitions in section 2. A colleague suggests raising the temperature. What is wrong with that suggestion?

options.A: Raising max_tokens would let the full contract fit as input
options.B: Temperature should be lowered instead to fit more text
options.C: Temperature changes which token is selected, not how much input fits; this is a capacity problem that needs both sections in the same request, or a deliberate split that carries the needed state
options.D: Nothing; higher temperature lets the model read more text

questions.explanation: Temperature selects; the window holds. Sampling settings, latency improvements and output caps all act on generation, not on input capacity. On Claude 4.7 and later, non-default temperature is rejected anyway.

questions.question: Roughly how many English characters does one Claude token represent?

options.A: Exactly one word
options.B: About 20 characters
options.C: Exactly one character
options.D: About 3.5 characters, varying by language

questions.explanation: Tokens map to words, subwords, characters or bytes. Input, output and thinking are all measured in tokens, which is the unit you are billed in and limited by. Use the token counting endpoint rather than estimating for anything important.

questions.question: What is 'context rot'?

options.A: The degradation of accuracy and recall as a context window fills, because the window behaves as working memory rather than storage
options.B: The deletion of old messages by the API after a timeout
options.C: Corruption of cached prompts over time
options.D: A security attack that edits the system prompt

questions.explanation: A bigger window holds more but does not make every token equally attended. Keep the window focused: prune spent tool output, compact, and retrieve only what is relevant.

questions.question: Select the TWO statements about request settings that are accurate.

options.A: A larger context window makes wording more consistent between runs
options.B: max_tokens caps how long the response may run; it does not change how much input fits
options.C: Effort controls how many tokens the model spends reasoning and responding; it does not enlarge the context window
options.D: Raising temperature lets more input fit in the window

questions.explanation: Treat each dial as a separate machine: sampling selects tokens, the window bounds input, max_tokens bounds output, effort bounds deliberation. Wrong answers in this area apply a real dial to the wrong problem.

questions.question: A team has 15 labelled examples of exactly the output they want and a model that keeps getting edge cases wrong. Which approach should they try first?

options.A: Train a custom model on the 15 examples
options.B: Put a selection of those examples in the prompt (few-shot)
options.C: Warn users to avoid the edge cases
options.D: Store the examples in a database the model never reads

questions.explanation: Examples in the prompt are the cheapest mechanism that fits: nothing needs to be built before trying it. Reaching for training or retrieval infrastructure spends the same information through a far more expensive channel.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the context window?

options.A: It applies only to output tokens
options.B: It limits only the user's latest message
options.C: It bounds the total tokens a single request can carry, including system prompt, messages, tool definitions, images, documents, and the response itself
options.D: It is unlimited when prompt caching is enabled

questions.explanation: Everything competes for one budget. Cached prefixes still occupy it: caching changes price, not space.

questions.question: On Claude Opus 4.7 and later, a migrated integration sends temperature: 0.2 and gets an error. Why?

options.A: The account has exceeded its temperature quota
options.B: Temperature is only allowed when streaming
options.C: Temperature must be an integer
options.D: Non-default sampling parameters (temperature, top_p, top_k) are rejected with a 400 on these models; remove them and steer behaviour through prompting

questions.explanation: Sampling parameters are deprecated on Claude 4.7 and later. Migration breaks like this show up loudly as 400s; plan for them when changing model IDs.

questions.question: What distinguishes latency from throughput in an integration?

options.A: They are synonymous when concurrency is fixed
options.B: Throughput measures the size of the context window
options.C: Latency is time to complete one request; throughput is volume completed per unit time
options.D: Latency applies to input tokens and throughput to output tokens

questions.explanation: Latency is per-request duration; throughput is aggregate rate. They are optimized differently and frequently trade against each other.

questions.question: An offline enrichment job must finish a large queue as fast as possible overall. Which optimization matters most?

options.A: Minimizing the latency of each individual call
options.B: Enabling streaming so results appear sooner
options.C: Maximizing throughput via concurrency and batching within rate limits
options.D: Raising the token ceiling on every request

questions.explanation: When nothing waits on any single response, aggregate completion rate is the objective, and concurrency plus batching within the rate limit is how it is raised.

questions.question: Raising concurrency improved throughput up to a point, after which per-request latency climbed sharply and errors appeared. What is the most likely explanation?

options.A: Streaming was implicitly disabled at high concurrency
options.B: Higher concurrency forces a lower model tier
options.C: The context window shrinks as concurrency rises
options.D: Concurrency has exceeded the account's rate limits, producing throttling and queueing

questions.explanation: Throughput scales with concurrency only until the rate limit binds; beyond it requests are throttled and queue, which lengthens latency and surfaces rate-limit errors.

questions.question: Which change reduces perceived latency for a user without reducing the total tokens generated?

options.A: Streaming the response so output renders as it is produced
options.B: Raising the token ceiling
options.C: Adding more concurrent workers to the request pool
options.D: Submitting the request through batch processing

questions.explanation: Streaming does not shorten generation but lets the user begin reading immediately, which is what perceived latency measures. Batching and worker counts do not help a single waiting user.

questions.question: Which factor most directly influences time-to-first-token as opposed to total response time?

options.A: The requested maximum output length
options.B: The number of distinct tools defined on the request
options.C: Whether results are written to a database afterward
options.D: The size of the input that must be processed before generation begins

questions.explanation: Time-to-first-token is dominated by processing the input prefix, which is why caching a large prefix improves it. Output length governs total duration, not the initial delay.

questions.question: Select the TWO statements that correctly describe latency and throughput optimization.

options.A: Increasing concurrency reliably reduces the latency of each individual request
options.B: Throughput is unaffected by account rate limits
options.C: A lighter model tier generally reduces per-request latency
options.D: Caching a large static prefix can improve time-to-first-token on repeat requests

questions.explanation: Lighter tiers respond faster and cached prefixes shorten the pre-generation phase. Concurrency raises aggregate throughput without shortening any single request, and rate limits cap throughput directly.

questions.question: A real-time moderation check must return a verdict before a message is posted. Which priority should govern the configuration?

options.A: Throughput, since moderation runs on every message
options.B: Latency, since the user's action is blocked until the verdict returns
options.C: Cost, since moderation is high volume
options.D: Reasoning depth, since moderation is nuanced

questions.explanation: A synchronous gate in the user's path is latency-bound: the check must return fast enough not to stall the interaction, which typically points to a lighter tier and a tight output budget.

questions.question: Latency is the stated problem and output quality is fine. Which lever avoids changing what the model produces?

options.A: Rewriting the prompt to ask for different content
options.B: Switching to a smaller tier
options.C: Streaming, caching the stable prefix, or fast mode where available, rather than a smaller tier
options.D: Raising max_tokens

questions.explanation: A smaller tier changes the output. Streaming improves perceived latency, caching shortens time to first token, and fast mode makes the same model generate faster. Lowering effort also cuts latency but trades some thoroughness, so measure it.

questions.question: For the task 'simple intent classification', which model-selection approach best balances cost, latency, and quality?

options.A: Match model choice to task complexity and latency needs — using smaller/faster models for simple, high-volume work and reserving the most capable model for genuinely complex reasoning
options.B: Model choice has no measurable effect on cost or latency
options.C: Always default to the most capable (and most expensive) model regardless of task complexity
options.D: Always use the cheapest model regardless of accuracy requirements

questions.explanation: Cost-effective architecture matches model capability to task difficulty rather than defaulting to one tier for everything.

questions.question: For 'a voice-of-customer sentiment tagger', which is the strongest signal that a smaller/cheaper model tier would be sufficient rather than the largest available model?

options.A: The task is high-volume and relatively simple/pattern-based, with well-defined expected outputs, rather than requiring deep multi-step reasoning
options.B: The task involves any use of the word 'analysis' anywhere in its description
options.C: The application is used by external customers rather than internal staff
options.D: The team prefers using fewer distinct API calls

questions.explanation: Task complexity and reasoning depth — not audience or terminology — is the key signal for whether a smaller, cheaper model tier is sufficient.

questions.question: A high-volume routing classifier assigns tickets to one of eight queues, and accuracy is already acceptable on a light tier. What follows?

options.A: Alternate tiers to balance cost and quality
options.B: Enable extended thinking to improve consistency
options.C: Move to the most capable tier to protect against edge cases
options.D: Keep the light tier, since it already meets the quality bar and a more capable tier would add cost and latency without a needed gain

questions.explanation: When a light tier already meets the quality bar, additional capability adds cost and latency without benefit. Tier selection is validated empirically, not by defaulting upward.

questions.question: What is the most defensible way to choose a tier for a new recurring workload?

options.A: Choose the cheapest tier and accept the resulting quality
options.B: Evaluate candidate tiers against a representative labelled sample and pick the cheapest that clears the quality bar
options.C: Choose the most capable tier and downgrade only if costs become a problem
options.D: Choose based on the tier used by a previous unrelated project

questions.explanation: Measuring candidates against representative data identifies the cheapest tier that meets requirements. The alternatives substitute habit or assumption for evidence.

questions.question: Which workload most justifies the most capable available tier?

options.A: Normalizing postal addresses into a fixed format
options.B: Detecting whether a message contains a phone number
options.C: Analysing an ambiguous contract clause where a wrong reading carries legal consequence
options.D: Converting a date string between two formats

questions.explanation: Capability earns its cost where judgment is genuinely difficult and errors are expensive. Deterministic formatting and simple detection do not benefit.

questions.question: A team wants a light tier for cost but needs stronger performance on one narrow subtask. Which design addresses this best?

options.A: Send every request to both tiers and compare outputs
options.B: Keep the light tier and accept the weaker results
options.C: Escalate only the narrow subtask to a more capable tier, keeping the light tier for the rest
options.D: Move the whole workload to the capable tier

questions.explanation: Tier choice can be made per step rather than per application, so escalating only the demanding subtask captures most of the saving while meeting the quality requirement.

questions.question: What does moving to a more capable tier generally cost?

options.A: Nothing; capability improves at constant price and speed
options.B: Only context window size
options.C: Higher per-token price and typically slower responses
options.D: Only the ability to use tools

questions.explanation: Capability trades against price and speed, which is why tier selection is a per-workload decision rather than a single global default.

questions.question: After a tier change, a team wants confidence that quality has not regressed. What is the right instrument?

options.A: Spot-checking a handful of outputs by eye
options.B: Monitoring the error rate of HTTP responses
options.C: Comparing average response length before and after
options.D: Running a fixed evaluation set through both tiers and comparing scored results

questions.explanation: A held-out evaluation set scored consistently is what makes a tier comparison meaningful. Length and HTTP errors say nothing about answer quality.

questions.question: Select the TWO signals that a cheaper tier is likely sufficient for a task.

options.A: The task is narrow and pattern-based with well-defined expected outputs
options.B: The task requires weighing several ambiguous, interacting considerations
options.C: A representative sample shows the light tier matching the capable tier's accuracy
options.D: Errors on the task are costly and difficult to detect downstream

questions.explanation: Narrow, well-specified work and measured parity both support the cheaper tier. Genuine ambiguity and high error cost argue for more capability.

questions.question: Two models are being compared for an agentic task. The cheaper one has half the per-token price but often needs extra turns and retries. What metric should decide?

options.A: Cost per completed task, including retries and failures, priced on the hardest cases
options.B: Public benchmark rank
options.C: Price per token only
options.D: Average response length

questions.explanation: A stronger model can use fewer turns. Compare on cost per completed task, and price the hardest tenth: a failed task bills its tokens, the retry and the downstream damage.

questions.question: A product spec lists features but gives no figures for acceptable latency, cost or quality. What should happen before choosing a model?

options.A: Pick the model at the top of a public leaderboard
options.B: Obtain all three targets (quality bar, latency ceiling, cost per unit of work), then choose against them
options.C: Pick a mid-range model as a compromise
options.D: Pick the newest model by default

questions.explanation: No model choice is defensible until the quality bar, the wait and the spend are known. A public benchmark measures work that is not yours and sets no threshold.

questions.question: A working integration moves to a newer model. The request shape still validates. What should the team do before switching production traffic?

options.A: Only update the model ID string
options.B: Re-baseline: run the evaluation set, re-check settings that may now be rejected (sampling, thinking budgets, prefill), and re-measure token counts and cost
options.C: Rewrite all prompts from scratch
options.D: Nothing; a valid request shape means a drop-in replacement

questions.explanation: A release changes behaviour, not just an identifier. Some breaks are loud 400s; others are quiet cost or behaviour shifts, such as instructions written for an older model being followed too literally or a new tokenizer changing counts.

questions.question: What is the difference between a deprecated model and a retired model?

options.A: They mean the same thing
options.B: A deprecated model fails immediately
options.C: A deprecated model still works but has an announced retirement date and a recommended replacement; a retired model is unavailable and requests to it fail
options.D: A retired model still works at a discount

questions.explanation: Deprecated means plan your migration; retired means it is already too late. Anthropic notifies customers with at least 60 days' notice for publicly released models.

questions.question: How can a team find every remaining place its applications call a model scheduled for retirement?

options.A: Check the SDK version number
options.B: Ask the model which version it is
options.C: Wait for requests to start failing
options.D: Audit API usage (for example, the Console usage export broken down by API key and model) and search configuration for the model ID

questions.explanation: A usage audit locates call sites by key and model, which is faster and more reliable than waiting for failures after the retirement date.

questions.question: A team's per-token price is unchanged after a model upgrade, but monthly spend rose about 20%. What is a likely explanation?

options.A: The new model uses a different tokenizer, so the same text produces more tokens; re-baseline token counts with the counting endpoint
options.B: Caching stops working after upgrades
options.C: Output tokens became free and input tokens doubled
options.D: Prices are secretly higher than published

questions.explanation: Tokenizers can change between generations, so the same text can cost more tokens. Count tokens on representative inputs before and after a migration.

questions.question: Why can instructions written for an older model cost more on a newer one even when outputs still pass?

options.A: Newer models follow instructions more literally, so stale verbose or 'be thorough' instructions can be obeyed fully, increasing output and spend
options.B: Instructions are billed as output tokens
options.C: Newer models charge for reading instructions twice
options.D: Older instructions are rejected with a 400

questions.explanation: Migration includes auditing prompts written for the previous model; remove cruft that no longer serves a purpose and re-measure.

questions.question: Which TWO factors most directly affect the per-request cost of a Claude API call?

options.A: The number of input and output tokens processed
options.B: Which model is used (different models have different per-token pricing)
options.C: The number of employees at the company making the call
options.D: The programming language of the client application

questions.explanation: Cost scales with token volume (input + output) and the chosen model's pricing tier; the client language and company size are irrelevant to API cost.

questions.question: Output tokens are generally priced differently from input tokens for Claude models. What is the practical implication for cost optimization?

options.A: Output length has no bearing on cost, only input length matters
options.B: Constraining unnecessarily long or verbose outputs (e.g., via explicit formatting instructions) can meaningfully reduce cost, since output tokens are typically priced higher than input tokens
options.C: Input and output tokens always cost exactly the same
options.D: Only the Batches API has token-based pricing; synchronous calls are flat-rate

questions.explanation: Output tokens are typically more expensive per-token than input tokens, so controlling output verbosity is a meaningful cost lever.

questions.question: A classification endpoint should return one of five labels but often returns a paragraph of justification. What is the most efficient correction?

options.A: Raise the output ceiling so nothing is truncated
options.B: Post-process the paragraph to extract the label
options.C: Move to a more capable tier
options.D: Instruct the model to return only the label, and set a low output ceiling as a guard

questions.explanation: Preventing unnecessary generation is cheaper than paying for it and discarding it. A low ceiling backs up the instruction against occasional verbosity.

questions.question: What does the maximum-tokens parameter actually control?

options.A: A target length the model attempts to match
options.B: The total of input plus output tokens for the request
options.C: The size of the context window available to the model
options.D: An upper bound on generated output, beyond which generation halts

questions.explanation: It is a hard ceiling on generation, not a target. Set it too low and responses are cut off mid-sentence rather than shortened gracefully.

questions.question: Why is relying solely on a low output ceiling a poor way to obtain concise answers?

options.A: The ceiling is ignored when a system prompt is present
options.B: Lower ceilings raise the per-token price
options.C: The ceiling applies only to streaming responses
options.D: The ceiling truncates mid-generation rather than producing a complete shorter answer

questions.explanation: A ceiling stops generation abruptly wherever it lands. Conciseness comes from instructing the desired length, with the ceiling serving only as a backstop.

questions.question: Select the TWO practices that reduce output-token spend without degrading the delivered result.

options.A: Setting the token ceiling far below the needed length so responses are always short
options.B: Requesting only the fields the caller actually consumes rather than a full narrative
options.C: Enabling extended thinking on every request to improve efficiency
options.D: Specifying a concrete length appropriate to where the output is displayed

questions.explanation: Asking only for what is consumed, at a length matched to its destination, cuts waste without loss. An under-set ceiling truncates mid-sentence, and always-on reasoning adds billed tokens.

questions.topic: Agent Build Options (Tool Runner, Agent SDK, Managed Agents)
questions.question: What is the key difference between the API SDK's Tool Runner and the Claude Agent SDK?

options.A: They are two names for the same package
options.B: The Tool Runner is hosted by Anthropic while the Agent SDK must be self-hosted
options.C: The Agent SDK cannot use custom tools or MCP servers
options.D: The Tool Runner loops over tools you define on the regular Messages API; the Agent SDK packages the Claude Code harness with built-in file, shell and search tools, hooks, subagents and permissions

questions.explanation: Both are harness-only (you host them). The Tool Runner automates request, execute, loop for your own tools. The Agent SDK is Claude Code as a library: query(), built-in tools, context management, hooks, subagents, permission modes and sessions.

questions.topic: Agent Build Options (Tool Runner, Agent SDK, Managed Agents)
questions.question: A team wants Anthropic to run the agent loop and host a per-session sandbox where bash and file operations execute, with versioned agent configurations. Which option fits?

options.A: Managed Agents, where the agent is a stored, versioned resource and each session gets a hosted container
options.B: The Tool Runner, which includes a hosted sandbox
options.C: The Message Batches API
options.D: A manual while-loop over the Messages API

questions.explanation: Managed Agents is the option that supplies both the harness and the deployment. The manual loop, Tool Runner and Agent SDK all leave hosting to you.

questions.topic: Agent Build Options (Tool Runner, Agent SDK, Managed Agents)
questions.question: A regulated team must keep conversation and tool data within systems they control, and a fully hosted agent runtime stores session state server-side. How should this requirement be treated?

options.A: As irrelevant, because the model provider is responsible for compliance
options.B: As a constraint that removes non-compliant options before anything else is compared; choose the deployment the rule permits, then reduce its operational cost
options.C: As something to resolve after a pilot proves the value
options.D: As one factor to balance against delivery speed

questions.explanation: Residency, retention and regulatory rules define the feasible set; they never compete inside it. A hosted runtime that stores session data is ruled out wherever the rule forbids that, whatever its convenience.

questions.topic: Agent Build Options (Tool Runner, Agent SDK, Managed Agents)
questions.question: After adopting the Agent SDK, a developer also writes their own loop to manage conversation history 'for safety'. What is the main problem?

options.A: Nothing; duplicate history improves reliability
options.B: Custom history makes prompt caching free
options.C: Half-adoption creates two sources of truth for the same conversation state; once a framework owns the loop, dispatch and history, let it
options.D: The SDK will refuse to run if a second history exists

questions.explanation: Hand-writing part of what the framework owns produces two owners for one piece of state, and they drift. A custom loop is justified by a constraint the library cannot meet, not by caution.

questions.topic: Agent Build Options (Tool Runner, Agent SDK, Managed Agents)
questions.question: An Agent SDK run can end in success, by hitting the turn ceiling, by hitting the spend ceiling, or with an error. How should application code decide what happened?

options.A: Search the final text for the word 'done'
options.B: Count the number of tool calls made
options.C: Assume success if no exception was raised
options.D: Branch on the result's subtype field, not on the final text, which exists only on success

questions.explanation: Structured result subtypes distinguish success from max-turns, max-budget and execution errors, and cost and usage arrive on all of them. Parsing prose for completion is fragile.

questions.topic: Agent Build Options (Tool Runner, Agent SDK, Managed Agents)
questions.question: Which situation best justifies writing a custom agent loop over the raw Messages API instead of using an SDK harness?

options.A: A hard requirement the harness cannot meet, such as a bespoke approval protocol between specific tool calls
options.B: The team has not used the SDK before
options.C: The agent uses more than one tool
options.D: The team wants fewer lines of code

questions.explanation: A custom loop charges you for context management, parallel tool handling, retries and exit conditions as code you maintain. Adopt it for a constraint the library cannot satisfy, not out of unfamiliarity.

questions.topic: Agent Frameworks (LangGraph / Strands) vs Native SDK
questions.question: What is the relationship between third-party agent frameworks like LangGraph or Strands and Anthropic's own Claude Agent SDK?

options.A: They are mutually exclusive; using one means Claude cannot be used with the other
options.B: They represent alternative or complementary orchestration approaches for building agents with Claude, each with their own abstractions for control flow and state, layered on top of the same underlying model and API
options.C: LangGraph and Strands are Anthropic products that replace the Claude Agent SDK
options.D: They are only usable for non-Claude models

questions.explanation: Third-party frameworks and the native Agent SDK are alternative/complementary orchestration layers on top of the same underlying Claude API.

questions.topic: Agent Frameworks (LangGraph / Strands) vs Native SDK
questions.question: A team chooses to build a multi-agent system using LangGraph instead of the native Claude Agent SDK. What does this decision primarily reflect?

options.A: A requirement imposed by Anthropic for all production agents
options.B: An inability to use Claude's tool-use feature at all
options.C: A fundamentally different set of agent-design principles that don't apply to SDK-based agents
options.D: A build-tooling/orchestration choice layered on top of the same core agent-design principles (tool-use loops, subagents, memory) that apply to SDK-based agents

questions.explanation: The underlying agent-design principles remain the same; framework choice is an orchestration/tooling decision layered on top.

questions.topic: Agent Frameworks (LangGraph / Strands) vs Native SDK
questions.question: Which statement about agent design patterns (e.g., manager/subagent decomposition, memory management) across the native Agent SDK vs. third-party frameworks is most accurate?

options.A: These patterns are conceptually consistent across implementations, even though specific syntax and abstractions differ between the native SDK and frameworks like LangGraph or Strands
options.B: These patterns only apply to the native Claude Agent SDK and have no equivalent in third-party frameworks
options.C: Third-party frameworks cannot implement subagent architectures
options.D: Memory management is impossible outside the native SDK

questions.explanation: The core design patterns transfer conceptually across implementations; only the specific syntax/abstractions differ.

questions.topic: Agent Frameworks (LangGraph / Strands) vs Native SDK
questions.question: A team is already deeply invested in an existing LangGraph-based orchestration pipeline for multiple LLM providers and wants to add Claude as one of the models. What is a reasonable interpretation of this scenario?

options.A: LangGraph can integrate Claude as one of the models within its existing orchestration graph, without requiring a rewrite onto the native Agent SDK
options.B: They must abandon LangGraph and rebuild entirely on the Claude Agent SDK
options.C: Claude can only be used through its own SDK, never through third-party orchestration
options.D: This is not possible; LangGraph cannot be used with Claude

questions.explanation: Third-party frameworks can incorporate Claude as one of their supported models without forcing a rewrite onto Anthropic's native SDK.

questions.topic: Agent Frameworks (LangGraph / Strands) vs Native SDK
questions.question: What is a reasonable factor in choosing the native Claude Agent SDK over a third-party framework like Strands for a new, Claude-only agent project?

options.A: There is no valid reason to ever choose the native SDK
options.B: Tighter, more direct alignment with Claude-specific features without an additional abstraction layer, if the project doesn't need multi-provider or framework-specific orchestration features
options.C: Third-party frameworks cannot be used with Claude under any circumstances
options.D: The native SDK is the only option that supports tool use at all

questions.explanation: For Claude-only projects without a need for multi-provider orchestration, the native SDK avoids an extra abstraction layer.

questions.topic: Agent Frameworks (LangGraph / Strands) vs Native SDK
questions.question: Is it accurate that using a third-party agent framework means you can no longer apply concepts like stopping conditions, guardrails, or context management to your agent?

options.A: False, but only if the framework is LangGraph specifically
options.B: False — these are general agent-design concepts that still apply regardless of which orchestration layer (native SDK or third-party framework) implements the agent loop
options.C: True — these concepts are exclusive to the native Claude Agent SDK
options.D: True, but only for stopping conditions specifically

questions.explanation: Stopping conditions, guardrails, and context management are general agent-design concepts applicable regardless of the orchestration layer used.

questions.topic: Agent Frameworks (LangGraph / Strands) vs Native SDK
questions.question: Which requirement most favors a third-party agent framework over the native SDK?

options.A: The agent performs a single well-understood step
options.B: The project must remain portable across several model providers
options.C: The team wants the closest possible access to Claude-specific capabilities
options.D: The project targets Claude exclusively and needs minimal abstraction

questions.explanation: Multi-provider portability is a framework's central value. Claude-only projects wanting direct access to platform features are better served by the native SDK.

questions.topic: Agent Frameworks (LangGraph / Strands) vs Native SDK
questions.question: What is the main cost of introducing an agent framework on top of the model API?

options.A: Frameworks wrap the same loop but obscure the prompts and responses underneath, which makes debugging harder; understand what it does and reduce layers going into production
options.B: Frameworks cannot call Claude
options.C: Frameworks remove the need for evaluation
options.D: Frameworks always double token usage

questions.explanation: Frameworks charge in visibility. Starting directly against the API, understanding what the abstraction does, and keeping layers to a minimum in production keeps failures diagnosable.

questions.question: A review pipeline's final stage keeps attributing findings to the wrong file, because each worker returns a prose summary that the last stage re-parses. What fixes this?

options.A: Ask the final stage to reconstruct locations more carefully
options.B: Have each worker write a structured record where the observation is made: file path, symbol, line range and evidence snippet
options.C: Increase the final stage's context window
options.D: Concatenate all worker transcripts and pass them to the final stage

questions.explanation: No later stage can recover a fact nobody recorded. Whichever stage sees a detail must write it down in a defined shape; reconstructing it downstream from prose is guesswork.

questions.question: A downstream stage sometimes starts before the stage producing its input has finished. What is the most reliable fix?

options.A: Add a fixed delay before the downstream stage runs
options.B: Let the downstream stage generate output and prune it afterwards
options.C: Gate the downstream stage on an explicit status and manifest that the producing stage sets when it completes
options.D: Have the downstream stage look for the word 'complete' in the producer's output

questions.explanation: Sequencing must rest on a status the producer sets, never on words found in prose or on timing guesses.

questions.question: A coordinator delegates a subtask to a subagent but the subagent repeats work another subagent already did and misses a key source. What was most likely missing?

options.A: Access to the coordinator's full conversation history
options.B: A higher maximum turn count
options.C: A larger model for the subagent
options.D: A complete launching prompt: objective, output format, tools and sources to use, and the boundary of the task, since the prompt is the subagent's only channel in

questions.explanation: A subagent starts with no parent conversation. Whatever its launching prompt omits is simply absent, so short delegation instructions produce workers that misread the assignment or duplicate each other.

questions.question: A 40-minute agent task with several named milestones is sometimes interrupted and must restart from scratch. What design change addresses this?

options.A: Persist state at each milestone to external storage and reload it when the run resumes
options.B: Raise the process timeout so interruptions happen less often
options.C: Run a duplicate copy in parallel as a backup
options.D: Keep all progress in the conversation context only

questions.explanation: Resumability needs state that outlives the process. A longer timeout only makes interruption rarer; in-context state dies with the session.

questions.question: Select the TWO accurate statements about context in a coordinator/subagent design where each subagent starts with a fresh context (it is not a fork of the coordinator's conversation).

options.A: A subagent's own tool calls and results stay in its context; only its final message returns to the coordinator
options.B: Separate agents share one context window, so isolation saves no tokens
options.C: Anything the subagent needs from earlier work must be passed explicitly in its launching prompt
options.D: Subagents automatically see the coordinator's full conversation

questions.explanation: Isolation keeps material out of the coordinator's window, which is the point of delegation, and the price is visibility: a fresh subagent loads its own system prompt and project context but none of the coordinator's turns, so the launching prompt is the only channel in and the final message the only channel out. (A fork is the exception: it inherits the conversation, but its tool calls still stay out of the coordinator's window.)

questions.question: For an autonomous coding agent editing files, which design choice best balances autonomy with safety?

options.A: Give the agent unrestricted permissions so it never has to pause for approval
options.B: Define clear stopping conditions and human-approval checkpoints for high-impact actions, while allowing autonomy for low-risk steps
options.C: Disable all logging to improve performance
options.D: Never allow the agent to use any tools

questions.explanation: Well-designed agents combine autonomy for low-risk steps with explicit guardrails (approval checkpoints, stopping conditions) for higher-impact or irreversible actions.

questions.question: An agent can issue refunds. Which guardrail design is soundest?

options.A: Instruct the agent in its system prompt never to exceed the refund limit
options.B: Use a more capable model tier so the limit is respected reliably
options.C: Enforce the limit in the refund service itself and require human approval above a threshold
options.D: Review a log of refunds weekly and reverse any that were incorrect

questions.explanation: Limits must be enforced where the action executes, since prompt instructions are not a security boundary. Human approval above a threshold bounds the damage of any single decision.

questions.question: Why is a prompt instruction an inadequate guardrail for a high-impact action?

options.A: Instructions influence behavior but cannot guarantee it, so they do not constitute enforcement
options.B: Instructions are stripped from requests that define tools
options.C: Instructions only apply to the first turn of a conversation
options.D: Prompt instructions cannot describe constraints precisely enough

questions.explanation: Prompting shapes likely behavior; it does not make an action impossible. Anything that must not happen requires a technical control outside the model.

questions.question: Select the TWO controls that meaningfully bound the risk of an autonomous agent with write access.

options.A: Increasing the iteration limit so the agent can self-correct
