options.B: Scoping credentials so the agent can only reach the specific resources it needs
options.C: Adding a strongly worded warning to the system prompt
options.D: Requiring explicit human approval before irreversible operations

questions.explanation: Narrow credentials and approval gates on irreversible actions are enforceable controls. Prompt warnings are advisory, and more iterations expand rather than bound the blast radius.

questions.question: A requirement states an agent must never run a destructive database command. Which control satisfies it?

options.A: A firmly worded instruction in the system prompt
options.B: Logging every command and reviewing the log daily
options.C: Asking the agent to double-check its own commands before running them
options.D: A check that runs before the tool executes and can refuse the call, such as a pre-execution hook or a permission deny rule

questions.explanation: A refusal has to arrive while the call is still a request. Logs and reviews record an action that already happened, prompts change what is attempted rather than what is allowed, and self-checks add no independence.

questions.question: In the Claude Agent SDK, what is the general purpose of the core query()-style interface?

options.A: It only formats text for display and has no role in agent execution
options.B: It replaces the need for any tool definitions
options.C: It drives the agent loop — sending messages, handling tool calls, and managing turns — so developers don't have to hand-roll that control flow themselves
options.D: It is used exclusively for evaluation, not for running agents

questions.explanation: The Agent SDK's core interface manages the agent loop (message exchange, tool call handling, turn management) so developers can build agents without reimplementing this control flow from scratch.

questions.question: What does the Claude Agent SDK primarily provide over hand-rolling an agent against the raw API?

options.A: Ready-made handling of the agent loop, tool wiring, and session mechanics
options.B: Automatic elimination of token costs for tool calls
options.C: Exclusive access to models unavailable through the API
options.D: A guarantee that the agent cannot take unsafe actions

questions.explanation: The SDK packages the recurring scaffolding — loop control, tool integration, session handling — so teams are not rebuilding it. It confers no special model access or safety guarantee.

questions.question: A team is writing its third bespoke agent loop and finding the retry, tool-dispatch, and history-management code repetitive. What does this suggest?

options.A: They should move the loop into the system prompt
options.B: They should switch to batch processing
options.C: Agents are the wrong architecture for the problem
options.D: The repeated scaffolding is what the Agent SDK exists to provide

questions.explanation: Repeatedly rebuilding loop plumbing is the signal to adopt the SDK, which supplies that layer and leaves the team to write only domain-specific tools and policy.

questions.question: What role does context/memory management play in longer-running agent workflows?

options.A: Memory management only matters for single-turn, non-agentic requests
options.B: Agents automatically discard all context after each tool call, so no management is needed
options.C: As an agent takes many steps, developers often need strategies (e.g., summarizing prior steps, pruning irrelevant history) to keep the agent's context within limits and focused on relevant information
options.D: It is irrelevant since agents have unlimited context by default

questions.explanation: Long-running agents accumulate context over many steps; without active management (summarization, pruning) this can exceed context limits or dilute the model's focus with irrelevant history.

questions.question: A long-running agent's context fills with verbose tool outputs, crowding out its objective. What is the most effective remedy?

options.A: Summarize or truncate tool results before appending them, retaining only decision-relevant fields
options.B: Remove the objective from context to make room for tool output
options.C: Disable tools once the context reaches a threshold
options.D: Restart the agent from scratch whenever context grows large

questions.explanation: Compacting tool output at the point of ingestion keeps the goal and salient state resident. Dropping the objective or restarting discards exactly what must persist.

questions.question: Which state should an agent persist outside the conversation context?

options.A: Only the system prompt
options.B: Durable facts and progress that must survive compaction or a restart
options.C: Only the most recent tool result
options.D: Nothing; the context window is the correct place for all state

questions.explanation: Context is a working buffer that gets compacted and eventually lost. Anything that must survive belongs in external storage the agent can read back.

questions.question: Which TWO of the following are legitimate reasons to build a custom agent loop instead of relying entirely on default SDK behavior?

options.A: You need fine-grained control over intermediate steps, such as custom logging, guardrails, or human-approval checkpoints between tool calls
options.B: You want to prevent the agent from ever using more than one tool call in total
options.C: Your application has domain-specific stopping conditions or retry logic not covered by default behavior
options.D: Custom agent loops are required before any tool can be defined

questions.explanation: Custom loops are useful when you need extra control (logging, guardrails, human-in-the-loop) or nonstandard stopping/retry logic — not for arbitrarily restricting tool-call counts or as a prerequisite for tool definitions.

questions.question: What is the minimal cycle of a custom agent loop?

options.A: Call the model, execute any requested tools, append the results, and repeat until a termination condition holds
options.B: Send the request once and parse whatever comes back
options.C: Pre-plan every tool call, then execute them in a fixed order
options.D: Stream the response and terminate at the first content block

questions.explanation: The loop alternates model turns with tool execution, feeding results back until a stopping condition is met. Fixed pre-planned sequences are workflows, not agent loops.

questions.question: An agent loop occasionally runs indefinitely, repeating the same tool call. Which safeguard addresses this most directly?

options.A: A maximum-iteration cap combined with detection of repeated no-progress states
options.B: A more capable model tier
options.C: Removing the tool from the agent's toolset
options.D: Increasing the output token ceiling

questions.explanation: Non-terminating loops need an explicit bound plus progress detection so repeated identical states break out. Model capability does not guarantee termination.

questions.question: You're designing a multi-step travel-booking agent. How should tool access be scoped for this agent?

options.A: Tools should be assigned randomly to test robustness
options.B: Limited to only the tools actually necessary for its task (least privilege), reducing risk if the agent misbehaves or is manipulated
options.C: Tool scoping doesn't matter since agents never misuse tools
options.D: Given access to every tool in the organization by default for flexibility

questions.explanation: Least privilege: give the agent only the tools its task needs. A booking agent that can reach every tool in the organization turns one bad decision or one injected instruction into an incident with a much larger blast radius.

questions.question: Which characteristic of a task most strongly indicates an agentic design rather than a fixed pipeline?

options.A: The task has high request volume
options.B: The task requires structured JSON output
options.C: The task must complete within a strict latency budget
options.D: The steps needed cannot be enumerated in advance and depend on what is discovered

questions.explanation: Agency is warranted when the path is data-dependent and cannot be scripted ahead of time. Volume, output shape, and latency constraints do not by themselves imply an agent.

questions.question: You are designing a system with 2 specialized subagents coordinated by a manager/supervisor process. What is the primary benefit of this manager-subagent architecture?

options.A: It guarantees zero errors across the system
options.B: It allows decomposing a complex task into narrower, more focused subtasks, each handled by a subagent with tighter context and scope, improving reliability and manageability
options.C: It eliminates the need for any tool use
options.D: It removes the need for evaluation or testing

questions.explanation: Manager/subagent patterns decompose complex tasks so each subagent operates with a narrower, more focused context, generally improving reliability over one large monolithic agent.

questions.question: You're designing a multi-step travel-booking agent. How should this agent's overall goal best be broken down for reliability?

options.A: Into smaller, well-scoped subtasks (potentially via subagents) each with a narrower context, rather than one monolithic prompt trying to do everything at once
options.B: It should never be decomposed; one giant prompt is always more reliable
options.C: By decomposing it into subtasks written in a different programming language
options.D: Decomposition is irrelevant to agent reliability

questions.explanation: Decomposing a long multi-step goal into well-scoped subtasks, each with a narrower context, is more reliable than one monolithic prompt. Each piece can be tested and its output validated before the next step consumes it.

questions.question: What is the primary benefit of delegating subtasks to subagents rather than handling everything in one context?

options.A: Subagents remove the need for tool definitions
options.B: Each subagent works in its own context with a narrow remit, keeping the manager's context focused
options.C: Subagents eliminate token costs for delegated work
options.D: Subagents guarantee deterministic results

questions.explanation: Delegation partitions context and responsibility, so detail stays with the specialist and the manager retains an uncluttered view of overall progress.

questions.question: A manager agent coordinates six subagents and results are becoming inconsistent and hard to trace. Which corrective step is most useful?

options.A: Sharpen each subagent's remit and define the contract for what it returns to the manager
options.B: Merge all subagents back into a single agent
options.C: Give every subagent access to the full toolset for flexibility
options.D: Increase the manager's iteration limit

questions.explanation: Inconsistency across delegates usually traces to fuzzy responsibilities and undefined return contracts. Tightening both restores traceability without abandoning decomposition.

questions.question: Workers in a multi-agent system sometimes return malformed or contradictory output that flows downstream anyway. Which coordinator responsibility is missing?

options.A: Letting workers negotiate contradictions among themselves
options.B: Validating each worker's result against a defined contract before handing it on, with a per-worker budget and an agreed definition of done
options.C: Collapsing the system back into a single call
options.D: More detailed tracing of every worker

questions.explanation: The coordinator owns budget, validation and the handoff contract. Tracing and retries observe failures but intercept nothing on the way downstream; peer negotiation removes the component whose job it was.

questions.question: You're designing a multi-step travel-booking agent. What should determine when this agent decides it has completed its task and should stop?

options.A: Running forever until manually killed
options.B: An arbitrary fixed number of turns with no relation to task completion
options.C: Explicit, well-defined completion/stopping criteria tied to the task's actual goal (not just an arbitrary step limit) so the agent halts at the right point
options.D: Never stopping, since agents should always keep iterating

questions.explanation: Stopping should be tied to an explicit definition of done for the task (for example, booking confirmed and itinerary returned), backed by a safety ceiling on turns or spend. A bare step count with no relation to completion stops too early or too late.

questions.question: What should determine when an agent stops working on a task?

options.A: When the model stops requesting tools, with no additional bound
options.B: A fixed number of iterations chosen for every task alike
options.C: When the context window is exhausted
options.D: Whichever comes first: satisfaction of an explicit success condition, or a safety bound such as an iteration or budget cap

questions.explanation: Sound termination pairs a definition of done with a backstop bound, so the agent halts on success or on exhausting its allowance rather than drifting.

questions.question: Why is 'the model produced no further tool calls' insufficient as the sole stopping condition?

options.A: Tool calls are always present in every response
options.B: The absence of a tool call cannot be detected programmatically
options.C: The model may stop calling tools without having achieved the objective
options.D: Stopping requires an explicit stop sequence to be configured

questions.explanation: Ceasing to call tools indicates the model has nothing further to try, not that the goal was met. Verification against a success condition is what distinguishes completion from giving up.

questions.question: Why should an agent's exit conditions be enforced by the runtime rather than left to the model?

options.A: The model cannot read its own system prompt
options.B: Runtime limits make every task succeed
options.C: An agent loop ends when the model stops calling tools, but nothing guarantees that happens promptly on open-ended tasks; turn and spend ceilings that the runtime enforces bound the run and return distinct result states
options.D: Models are prohibited from deciding when a task is finished

questions.explanation: The model deciding it is finished is the normal exit and a useful signal, but not a guarantee: open-ended tasks can run long. Hard ceilings (maximum turns, maximum spend) bound the run and report which limit was hit, for example as error_max_turns or error_max_budget_usd results in the Agent SDK.

questions.topic: Workflow Patterns (Chaining, Routing, Parallelization, Orchestrator-Workers, Evaluator-Optimizer)
questions.question: A support system must send billing questions, technical faults and refund requests to three different prompts, each with its own tools. The categories are known in advance. Which workflow pattern fits?

options.A: Routing: classify the input first, then dispatch it to the specialised prompt for that category
options.B: An autonomous agent that decides at runtime which steps to take
options.C: One large prompt that handles all three categories with every tool attached
options.D: Evaluator-optimizer, looping until a grader approves the answer

questions.explanation: Known categories that each need different handling is the textbook case for routing. Variable input alone is a routing problem, not a reason for autonomy, and one giant prompt with every tool makes selection and evaluation harder.

questions.topic: Workflow Patterns (Chaining, Routing, Parallelization, Orchestrator-Workers, Evaluator-Optimizer)
questions.question: A marketing pipeline drafts copy, checks it against brand rules, then translates it. Each step consumes the previous step's output and the order never changes. Which pattern fits?

options.A: A fully autonomous agent with a planning step
options.B: Prompt chaining: a fixed sequence of calls, with a programmatic check (gate) between steps where useful
options.C: Orchestrator-workers, letting a lead model invent subtasks per request
options.D: Parallelization, running all three steps at once

questions.explanation: When the steps can be written down before the input arrives, code holds the plan and each model call does one job. Chaining trades a little latency for accuracy and lets you validate between steps.

questions.topic: Workflow Patterns (Chaining, Routing, Parallelization, Orchestrator-Workers, Evaluator-Optimizer)
questions.question: A code-migration tool must change an unpredictable number of files, and which files need changing depends on the repository it is given. Which pattern fits best?

options.A: Routing to one of three pre-written migration prompts
options.B: Parallelization over a hard-coded list of file paths
options.C: Orchestrator-workers: a lead model decides the subtasks from the input and delegates them to workers, then synthesises the results
options.D: Prompt chaining with a fixed list of five steps

questions.explanation: Orchestrator-workers fits when the subtasks themselves cannot be predicted and depend on the input. Chaining and fixed parallelization assume the decomposition is known in advance.

questions.topic: Workflow Patterns (Chaining, Routing, Parallelization, Orchestrator-Workers, Evaluator-Optimizer)
questions.question: A translation feature has clear, written quality criteria, and experience shows a second pass guided by specific feedback measurably improves the result. Which pattern fits?

options.A: Removing the criteria so the model is not constrained
options.B: An autonomous agent with unrestricted tool access
options.C: Routing, since translations vary by language
options.D: Evaluator-optimizer: one call generates, another evaluates against the criteria and returns feedback, looping a bounded number of times

questions.explanation: Evaluator-optimizer earns its cost only when evaluation criteria are explicit and another round demonstrably helps. Bound the loop so it cannot iterate forever.

questions.topic: Workflow Patterns (Chaining, Routing, Parallelization, Orchestrator-Workers, Evaluator-Optimizer)
questions.question: Select the TWO valid uses of the parallelization pattern.

options.A: Sectioning: splitting a task into independent parts that run at the same time and are combined afterwards
options.B: Voting: running the same task several times to get diverse outputs or a more confident judgement
options.C: Running steps in parallel when each step depends on the previous step's output
options.D: Running the same prompt twice to make an inherently sequential task finish faster

questions.explanation: Parallelization covers sectioning (independent subtasks) and voting (repeated attempts). It only helps when the pieces are genuinely independent; dependent steps must stay sequential.

questions.topic: Workflow Patterns (Chaining, Routing, Parallelization, Orchestrator-Workers, Evaluator-Optimizer)
questions.question: A team fanned a research task out to eight subagents. Token cost rose roughly tenfold, yet answer quality barely moved. What should they check first?

options.A: Whether the subtasks were ever independent; tightly coupled work pays the fan-out cost without any parallel benefit, so a single agent may fit better
options.B: Whether adding more subagents would finally show the benefit
options.C: Whether the subagents share a conversation history
options.D: Whether streaming was enabled on every subagent

questions.explanation: Multi-agent systems use many times the tokens of a single chat because every worker spends tokens on its own context. That cost is repaid only by genuinely parallel exploration (separate sources, material bigger than one window). Coupled work should not be fanned out.

questions.topic: Workflow Patterns (Chaining, Routing, Parallelization, Orchestrator-Workers, Evaluator-Optimizer)
questions.question: Ninety percent of an expense-approval flow follows fixed rules; a small remainder involves unusual cases that need judgement. What is the soundest design?

options.A: Make the whole system an autonomous agent so the edge cases are covered
options.B: Code the routine path as a fixed workflow and invoke a model-driven step only where the route forks unpredictably
options.C: Make the whole system a fixed workflow and reject every unusual case
options.D: Use one large prompt for everything to keep the architecture simple

questions.explanation: The workflow-or-agent decision belongs to each path, not the whole product. A single choice for everything either pays for planning on the settled majority or has no branch for the exceptions.

questions.topic: Workflow Patterns (Chaining, Routing, Parallelization, Orchestrator-Workers, Evaluator-Optimizer)
questions.question: Which test best decides whether a task should be built as a workflow or as an agent?

options.A: Whether the task can be enumerated as a JSON schema
options.B: Whether the number of tool calls is below ten
options.C: Whether the sequence of steps can be written down before the input arrives: if so, code holds the plan; if not, the model holds the plan and code holds the limits
options.D: Whether the request volume is high enough to justify an agent

questions.explanation: Workflows orchestrate the model through predefined code paths, so if the steps can be written down in advance, code holds the plan (a chain, router or other workflow). If the path cannot be hardcoded, an agent lets the model direct its own steps, while code still enforces turn caps, spend caps and validation.

questions.question: What is the key distinction between a 'workflow' and an 'agent' in the context of building with Claude?

options.A: There is no meaningful distinction; the terms are interchangeable
options.B: A workflow follows a predefined sequence of steps orchestrated by the developer, while an agent dynamically decides its own steps/tool calls based on the model's reasoning
options.C: Agents never use tools, while workflows always use tools
options.D: Workflows can only be built with the Claude Agent SDK, and agents cannot

questions.explanation: Workflows are developer-orchestrated fixed sequences; agents use the model to dynamically plan and execute steps, including deciding which tools to call and when to stop.

questions.question: You are designing a warehouse-robotics coordination agent and must decide between a fixed, developer-orchestrated workflow versus a fully autonomous agent that plans its own steps. Which factor most strongly favors the fixed-workflow approach?

options.A: The task is extremely open-ended with highly variable steps that can't be predicted in advance
options.B: There is no meaningful difference; the choice should be arbitrary
options.C: The team wants maximum flexibility for handling unexpected edge cases
options.D: The task's steps are well-understood, predictable, and rarely vary — reducing the value of dynamic planning while increasing the value of predictable, auditable execution

questions.explanation: Fixed, predictable, well-understood tasks generally favor a developer-orchestrated workflow (more predictable and auditable); highly variable, open-ended tasks favor a dynamically planning agent.

questions.question: A document pipeline always performs extract, then validate, then file — never varying. Which design is appropriate?

options.A: A manager agent with three subagents
options.B: An autonomous agent that decides the order at runtime
options.C: A developer-orchestrated workflow with the three steps in fixed sequence
options.D: A single request with all three instructions concatenated

questions.explanation: A known, invariant sequence is best expressed as an explicit workflow: more predictable, cheaper, and easier to debug than granting runtime discretion that is never needed.

questions.question: Select the TWO costs of choosing an autonomous agent where a fixed workflow would suffice.

options.A: Less predictable execution paths, making behavior harder to test and reason about
options.B: Loss of the ability to define custom tools
options.C: Inability to return structured output
options.D: Additional model calls for planning and reflection that the fixed path would not incur

questions.explanation: Unnecessary agency buys variability and extra deliberation cost. Neither tool definitions nor structured output is affected by the choice.

questions.question: In a helpdesk bot, you are considering asking the model to reason step by step before giving a final answer. What is the most accurate characterization of this technique's effect?

options.A: It should always be avoided because it wastes tokens with no benefit
options.B: It has no measurable effect on model behavior in any scenario
options.C: It can improve performance on multi-step reasoning tasks, at the cost of additional output tokens
options.D: It guarantees perfect output correctness regardless of task difficulty

questions.explanation: Reasoning through a problem before answering can improve performance on multi-step reasoning tasks, and those reasoning tokens are billed as output. On current models with thinking active, that reasoning happens in thinking blocks controlled by effort. Explicitly prompting for written-out step-by-step reasoning is the fallback when thinking is off, and on some of the newest models a prompt asking the model to write out its reasoning may be declined.

questions.question: A multi-step pricing calculation returns confidently wrong totals. Which prompting change is most likely to help?

options.A: Have the model reason through the intermediate steps before committing to the total (in its thinking, or by asking for step-by-step work where thinking is off)
options.B: Ask for the total only, to reduce distraction
options.C: Raise temperature to explore more possibilities
options.D: Repeat the question twice in the same prompt

questions.explanation: Working through intermediate steps improves multi-step arithmetic and shows where a wrong total diverged. On models with thinking active, this happens in thinking blocks, steered by effort. Prompting for step-by-step work is the fallback when thinking is off. Asking for only the final figure, raising temperature or repeating the question does nothing to make the calculation more reliable.

questions.question: An application needs the benefit of step-by-step reasoning but must return only a clean JSON verdict to its caller. What is the workable approach?

options.A: Abandon step-by-step reasoning, since it is incompatible with structured output
options.B: Keep the reasoning separate from the answer: let the model reason in thinking blocks (or, where thinking is off, a delimited reasoning section) and have the application extract only the final JSON
options.C: Instruct the model to reason silently without producing tokens
options.D: Send two unrelated requests and average the results

questions.explanation: Thinking arrives in separate thinking content blocks ahead of the response, so the text the application returns can be just the JSON verdict. Where thinking is off, asking for reasoning in a delimited section and the answer in a separate tagged section achieves the same separation. On the newest models, prompts asking the model to write out its reasoning in the response may be declined, so rely on thinking there.

questions.question: What is 'context drift' in the context of long conversations or long-running agents, and why does it matter?

options.A: It refers to the model's context window physically shrinking over time
options.B: It refers to the model's behavior gradually diverging from the original instructions/goal as irrelevant or conflicting information accumulates in context, which can be mitigated with periodic re-grounding or summarization
options.C: It only affects image inputs, never text
options.D: It is not a real phenomenon and cannot be observed or measured

questions.explanation: Context drift describes behavior degrading or diverging from original goals as context accumulates noise; mitigations include summarization and periodic reinforcement of key instructions.

questions.question: Late in a long conversation, the model begins ignoring a formatting rule stated in the first message. What is the most reliable fix?

options.A: Increase the output token ceiling
options.B: Switch to streaming so the rule is applied incrementally
options.C: Lower the temperature to zero
options.D: Restate the rule in the system prompt or near the current turn so it remains salient

questions.explanation: Instructions issued far back in a long exchange lose salience. Persisting them in the system prompt or refreshing them near the active turn keeps them in force.

questions.question: An assistant thread has accumulated several superseded decisions and the model keeps referring back to abandoned plans. What should the application do?

options.A: Raise the model tier so it can resolve the contradictions
options.B: Add an instruction to ignore anything contradictory
options.C: Append the newest decision more emphatically at the end
options.D: Compact the history into a summary that records only the decisions still in force

questions.explanation: Stale context competes with current intent. Rewriting history into a summary of what still holds removes the contradictory material instead of asking the model to arbitrate it.

questions.topic: Context Window Management (Clearing, Compaction, Context Rot)
questions.question: An agent's tool selection gets noticeably worse after about 40 tool calls, even though the window is far from full. What is the most effective remedy?

options.A: Merge all tools into one generic tool
options.B: Switch to a model with a larger context window
options.C: Rewrite the tool descriptions to be longer
options.D: Clear or compact spent tool output so stale results stop competing for attention, while protecting the current task state

questions.explanation: Degrading tool choice after a fixed number of turns is a window symptom (drift), not a schema symptom. A bigger window preserves every distraction at full detail; removing spent material is what helps.

questions.topic: Context Window Management (Clearing, Compaction, Context Rot)
questions.question: What is the difference between context editing (clearing) and compaction?

options.A: Clearing removes old tool results (or thinking) and leaves placeholders; compaction rewrites earlier history into a summary that replaces it
options.B: They are the same feature with two names
options.C: Both only affect the system prompt
options.D: Clearing summarises; compaction deletes

questions.explanation: Clearing is tuned by settings like how many recent tool uses to keep and which tools to exclude. Compaction is lossy by design and costs an extra summarisation step; when using it, append the full response content so compaction blocks are preserved.

questions.topic: Context Window Management (Clearing, Compaction, Context Rot)
questions.question: A rule ('never quote account numbers in full') is followed early in a long agent run but violated after several compactions. What is the right fix?

options.A: Ask the model to remember the rule
options.B: Move the rule outside what compaction can rewrite, such as the system prompt or a record re-injected each turn
options.C: Raise the compaction threshold so it runs less often
options.D: Restate the rule in a user message every few turns

questions.explanation: Compaction may drop anything inside the region it summarises. Changing the threshold alters frequency, not what a summary can discard, and restating the rule in the conversation puts it back inside the region being summarised.

questions.topic: Context Window Management (Clearing, Compaction, Context Rot)
questions.question: A knowledge base far larger than any context window is proposed as input to every prompt. What is the right approach?

options.A: Use the largest model so everything fits
options.B: Split the knowledge base across many parallel requests and merge the answers
options.C: Retrieve only the passages relevant to each query and include those
options.D: Limit the knowledge base to the first N documents

questions.explanation: Retrieval keeps the window focused on what the current question needs. Splitting a corpus across requests loses cross-references and multiplies cost.

questions.topic: Context Window Management (Clearing, Compaction, Context Rot)
questions.question: A later step in a multi-step workflow needs a decision made in an earlier step, but it behaves as if it never happened. What is the cause?

options.A: The model forgot because temperature was too high
options.B: Later steps always see everything in the same run
options.C: The earlier step's output was cached and therefore hidden
options.D: Context does not travel automatically; anything a later step or separate agent needs must be passed explicitly in its prompt

questions.explanation: Separate calls and separate agents share no context. Nothing carries forward unless something carries it.

questions.topic: Context Window Management (Clearing, Compaction, Context Rot)
questions.question: How does prompt engineering differ from context engineering?

options.A: Prompt engineering composes one exchange; context engineering decides what occupies the window across a whole session or agent run
options.B: They are identical
options.C: Prompt engineering is about model training
options.D: Context engineering only concerns images

questions.explanation: On one call they collapse together. On a long run, the question becomes what should be present at all, which no rewording of an instruction can answer.

questions.topic: Context Window Management (Clearing, Compaction, Context Rot)
questions.question: Select the TWO accurate statements about long-running agent context.

options.A: Compaction is lossless, so nothing important can be dropped
options.B: Spent context (tool output that already did its job) is still resent and billed every turn until it is removed
options.C: Cached tokens do not occupy any of the context window
options.D: A larger context window does not treat drift, because it keeps every distraction

questions.explanation: Caching changes price, not space, and compaction is lossy by design. Removing spent material is the lever for both cost and focus.

questions.question: A prompt currently includes 3 example(s) demonstrating the desired output format. What is the most likely effect of increasing the number of well-chosen examples (few-shot prompting) for a task with a specific, non-obvious output format?

options.A: It always guarantees perfect accuracy regardless of task difficulty
options.B: It will have no effect on output consistency
options.C: It generally improves the model's adherence to the desired format/style, up to a point of diminishing returns and increased token cost
options.D: It eliminates the need for any instructions in the prompt

questions.explanation: Few-shot examples typically improve format/style adherence for non-obvious tasks, though returns diminish and each example adds token cost.

questions.question: A team supplies twelve examples in a prompt and finds that quality stopped improving after the first few while cost kept rising. What does this indicate?

options.A: Twelve examples exceed the permitted maximum
options.B: Examples must always be supplied in odd numbers
options.C: Few-shot examples have diminishing returns, so the count should be tuned rather than maximized
options.D: Examples are only effective when placed after the user's question

questions.explanation: Examples help most at the margin of the first few. Beyond the point where quality plateaus, additional examples are paid input with no return.

questions.question: A classifier's few-shot examples all happen to be positive cases, and the model now over-predicts that class. What is the correct diagnosis?

options.A: The model tier is too light for the task
options.B: The examples need to be longer
options.C: The example set is unrepresentative, biasing the model toward the class it demonstrates
options.D: Few-shot prompting is unsuitable for classification

questions.explanation: Examples are treated as a sample of the expected distribution, so a skewed set teaches the skew. Coverage across classes matters more than example count.

questions.question: In a helpdesk bot, you are considering telling the model what NOT to do (e.g., 'do not include disclaimers'). What is the most accurate characterization of this technique's effect?

options.A: It can be useful but is often less reliable than positively specifying the desired behavior directly
options.B: It has no measurable effect on model behavior in any scenario
options.C: It guarantees perfect output correctness regardless of task difficulty
options.D: It should always be avoided because it wastes tokens with no benefit

questions.explanation: Negative instructions can be useful but is often less reliable than positively specifying the desired behavior directly

questions.question: A prompt lists eight things the model must not do, and compliance is inconsistent. What is the recommended reframing?

options.A: Repeat each prohibition three times for emphasis
options.B: State positively what the model should do, so the desired behavior is specified rather than merely bounded
options.C: Convert the prohibitions into a numbered list without other changes
options.D: Move the prohibitions into the user turn instead of the system prompt

questions.explanation: A list of prohibitions leaves the target behavior undefined. Describing the wanted output directly is more reliable than enumerating everything to avoid.

questions.question: Which rewrite best converts a negative instruction into a positive specification?

options.A: 'Do not speculate' becomes 'Do not guess or speculate under any circumstances'
options.B: 'Do not be vague' becomes 'Never write vaguely'
options.C: 'Do not use jargon' becomes 'Avoid all technical terminology at all costs'
options.D: 'Do not write long paragraphs' becomes 'Write in paragraphs of no more than three sentences'

questions.explanation: The effective rewrite replaces the prohibition with a concrete, checkable target. The others restate the same prohibition more forcefully without specifying what to produce.

questions.question: A system prompt written for an older model is full of CRITICAL and MUST NOT warnings. On a newer model, the behaviour over-triggers. What should change?

options.A: Add more capital letters
options.B: Repeat each warning twice
options.C: Soften the language and explain the reason, stating positively what to do
options.D: Remove all instructions

questions.explanation: Newer models follow instructions closely, so emphatic phrasing intended to overcome inattention causes over-application. Calm, reasoned instructions generalise better.

questions.question: In a helpdesk bot, you are considering explicitly specifying a maximum length or format for the response. What is the most accurate characterization of this technique's effect?

options.A: It helps produce consistent, predictable outputs and can reduce unnecessary token cost
options.B: It has no measurable effect on model behavior in any scenario
options.C: It guarantees perfect output correctness regardless of task difficulty
options.D: It should always be avoided because it wastes tokens with no benefit

questions.explanation: Output length constraints helps produce consistent, predictable outputs and can reduce unnecessary token cost

questions.question: Which instruction most reliably produces a summary that fits a fixed UI panel?

options.A: 'Summarize in no more than three sentences.'
options.B: 'Be concise but thorough.'
options.C: 'Keep it brief.'
options.D: 'Do not write too much.'

questions.explanation: A countable limit gives the model an unambiguous target. Subjective adjectives leave length to interpretation, and the last option sets two competing goals.

questions.question: An invoice extractor returns schema-valid JSON, but some totals do not match the line items. Which control catches this?

options.A: A stricter JSON schema
options.B: Recompute or cross-check the values outside the model (for example, sum the line items and compare), routing mismatches to human review
options.C: Switching to a larger model
options.D: A self-reported confidence field filled in by the model

questions.explanation: Schemas answer the shape question, not the truth question. A check catches a confident wrong answer only when its correctness rests on something established outside the model.

questions.question: Which verification approach is weakest for catching an answer that is confidently wrong?

options.A: Enforcing domain range rules in code
options.B: Recomputing derived values from source records
options.C: Asking the same model to rate its own confidence in the answer
options.D: Cross-checking against an authoritative database lookup

questions.explanation: Self-reported confidence, majority vote of the same model and self-grading fail exactly where the answer fails. Independent verification is arithmetic, lookups and range rules.

questions.question: Two credible sources give different revenue figures for the same quarter. How should an extraction pipeline represent this?

options.A: Keep the larger figure
options.B: Average the two figures
options.C: Ask the model to choose and drop the other
options.D: Carry both values with provenance (source, excerpt, timestamp) and mark the conflict for review

questions.explanation: Averaging invents a number nobody reported. Provenance and conflict are fields, so a reviewer can decide with the evidence in front of them.

questions.question: Downstream code crashes when a response contains an unexpected extra field or a missing optional value. What is the right parsing posture?

options.A: Parse defensively: tolerate unknown fields, keep absent, null and empty distinct, reject real type mismatches visibly, and log every rejection
options.B: Coerce missing values to defaults so nothing ever fails
options.C: Let the exception crash the pipeline
options.D: Silently drop any record that does not match exactly

questions.explanation: Defensive parsing survives surprises and still reports them. Silent drops are the worst failure, because the pipeline reports success while records disappear.

questions.question: A classifier must return one of the enum values 'APPROVED' or 'REJECTED', but occasionally returns 'Approved'. What is the safest handling?

options.A: Treat 'Approved' as a rejection
options.B: Compare enum values case-insensitively (or normalise case) on receipt, since capitalisation can vary without any error
options.C: Assume the API is broken
options.D: Retry until the exact casing appears

questions.explanation: Enum casing variation is a documented escape that carries no error and no special stop_reason. Normalise before comparing.

questions.question: An extraction pipeline routes every result on one global confidence threshold. Absent-but-optional fields, unreadable-but-required fields and out-of-scope documents are being mixed up. What is better?

options.A: Raise the global threshold
options.B: Lower the threshold so more items pass
options.C: Name and exemplify the distinct outcomes in the schema and prompt, and route each category to its own destination (accept, retry, human review, reject)
options.D: Retry until every field is filled

questions.explanation: These outcomes are different categories that no single confidence number separates. Forcing every field to fill turns a missing answer into an invented one.

questions.question: A prompt scores well on the development set but behaves poorly on live traffic. What should change?

options.A: Add more examples drawn from the clean development set
options.B: Change the sampling settings
options.C: Increase max_tokens
options.D: Add the failing live inputs to the evaluation set, and add rules for the messy cases they reveal (missing fields, conflicting passages, out-of-scope requests)

questions.explanation: The measured set must contain the inputs that fail. Optimising further on the distribution that already works does not reach the failing population.

questions.question: The task output is right but the model keeps inventing its own structure for the response. What is the most effective fix?

options.A: Show worked examples of the exact structure (or constrain it with structured outputs)
options.B: Repeat 'use the correct structure' more forcefully
options.C: Raise the temperature
options.D: Lengthen the task description

questions.explanation: Diagnose before re-prompting: invented structure wants examples or a constraint, drifting scope wants a more specific system prompt, and a broken input variant wants a rule covering it.

questions.question: Fields come back empty even though the documents contain the values, located in footnotes and cover letters. A teammate proposes adding 'never leave a field empty'. Why is that a poor fix?

options.A: It is a good fix; prohibitions are the most reliable instruction
options.B: A prohibition supplies no method; it pushes the model to invent values. Examples showing extraction from those locations change where the model looks
options.C: Because instructions are ignored in extraction tasks
options.D: Because empty fields are always correct

questions.explanation: Forbidding an empty value removes an outcome without providing a route to the right one, so the missing answer becomes a fabricated one.

questions.question: One call reads a document, extracts entities, judges risk and writes a summary, and quality is uneven across those parts. What should change?

options.A: Urge the model to be more thorough
options.B: Raise max_tokens
options.C: Split it into focused calls in sequence (prompt chaining), each fed the previous step's structured output
options.D: Change the temperature

questions.explanation: Each subtask gets the model's full attention in its own call, and each step can be evaluated separately.

questions.question: According to Anthropic's guidance, what makes an instruction effective?

options.A: Keeping the reason secret so the model does not argue
options.B: Repeating it several times
options.C: Writing it in capital letters with strong language
options.D: Saying what to do rather than what to avoid, and giving the reason, so the model can generalise to cases the instruction did not name

questions.explanation: Explanations generalise. Aggressive phrasing written for older models can cause newer ones to over-apply an instruction.

questions.question: Repeated fixes keep lengthening a prompt without fixing the problem. What is the right next step?

options.A: Name the specific failure from failing cases (input, expected vs actual), add the single missing technique, and measure
options.B: Relax the check that reports the failure
options.C: Rewrite the prompt from scratch
options.D: Keep adding instructions until it passes

questions.explanation: Iteration converges on specific evidence. Rewriting from scratch discards what already passed, and a prompt that only grows is a skipped diagnosis.

questions.question: In a helpdesk bot, you are considering assigning the model a specific persona or role (e.g., 'you are a senior security auditor'). What is the most accurate characterization of this technique's effect?

options.A: It should always be avoided because it wastes tokens with no benefit
options.B: It guarantees perfect output correctness regardless of task difficulty
options.C: It can help focus the model's tone, priorities, and framing for a task, though it does not grant the model new factual capabilities
options.D: It has no measurable effect on model behavior in any scenario

questions.explanation: Role prompting can help focus the model's tone, priorities, and framing for a task, though it does not grant the model new factual capabilities

questions.question: What does assigning a role such as 'you are a technical editor' primarily accomplish?

options.A: It grants access to specialized tools associated with that role
options.B: It restricts the model to a smaller vocabulary
options.C: It sets the perspective, vocabulary, and priorities the response is written from
options.D: It guarantees factual accuracy within that domain

questions.explanation: A role frames the perspective and register the model adopts. It neither confers capabilities nor guarantees correctness.

questions.question: A prompt assigns the role of 'senior security reviewer' but produces generic feedback. Which change is most likely to help?

options.A: Replace the role with a longer job description
options.B: Escalate to a more capable model tier
options.C: Pair the role with the specific review criteria and the output shape expected
options.D: Repeat the role assignment at the end of the prompt

questions.explanation: A role sets stance but does not convey what to look for. Combining it with concrete criteria and a defined output structure is what makes the feedback specific.

questions.question: A system prompt instructs Claude to 'always respond in valid JSON matching this schema,' but outputs are occasionally malformed. What is a recommended mitigation?

options.A: Remove the schema entirely since it isn't helping
options.B: Enforce the schema with structured outputs (output_config.format), give a concrete example, and keep application-side validation for what the schema cannot express
options.C: Switch to a lower-capability model to save cost
options.D: Ignore the malformed cases since JSON validity cannot be improved

questions.explanation: A prompt-level format request holds on the inputs you tested and slips on others. Structured outputs constrain generation so invalid JSON cannot be produced; validation on receipt still catches refusals, truncation and semantic errors.

questions.question: A JSON-returning endpoint fails roughly one call in two hundred on malformed output. What is the appropriate production posture?

options.A: Remove the schema so any output is acceptable
options.B: Assume the rate will fall as traffic grows
options.C: Treat the failure rate as acceptable and let exceptions propagate to users
options.D: Validate every response and retry on failure, since no prompting technique guarantees conformance

questions.explanation: Validation with a retry or review path is a required layer. Even with structured outputs, a refusal or a max_tokens truncation returns without usable structure, and schema-valid output can still be wrong, so the application must check stop_reason and validate before trusting a response.

questions.question: Which statement about structured outputs (output_config.format) is accurate?

options.A: It is the same as adding 'respond in JSON' to the prompt
options.B: It asks the model politely and retries on failure
options.C: It guarantees the values inside the JSON are factually correct
options.D: It compiles the JSON schema into a grammar that constrains generation, so the response always matches the declared shape unless it is refused or truncated

questions.explanation: Constrained generation removes the parse-failure class. It does not verify truth, and SDKs strip constraints (such as numeric ranges) the grammar cannot express, so validate on receipt.

questions.question: In a helpdesk bot, you are considering putting stable instructions in the system prompt and variable content in user turns. What is the most accurate characterization of this technique's effect?

options.A: It should always be avoided because it wastes tokens with no benefit
options.B: It guarantees perfect output correctness regardless of task difficulty
options.C: It helps keep static guidance separate from dynamic input, improving clarity and enabling prompt caching on the static portion
options.D: It has no measurable effect on model behavior in any scenario

questions.explanation: System vs. user prompt separation helps keep static guidance separate from dynamic input, improving clarity and enabling prompt caching on the static portion

questions.question: In a document-analysis product, where do the standing behavioral rules and the user's uploaded text belong?

options.A: Rules in the system prompt; document and question in the user turn
options.B: Both concatenated into the system prompt
options.C: Both concatenated into the user turn
options.D: Rules in the user turn; document in the system prompt

questions.explanation: Durable instructions belong in the system prompt where they persist and stay distinguishable, while per-request data belongs in the user turn.

questions.question: Why does mixing untrusted user-supplied text into the system prompt weaken an application?

options.A: System prompts have a stricter length limit than user turns
options.B: User text is not tokenized when placed in the system prompt
options.C: It blurs the boundary between the application's instructions and content that may attempt to override them
options.D: System prompts cannot be cached once they contain variable text

questions.explanation: Keeping untrusted content in the user turn preserves a clear separation between the operator's instructions and data, which is the foundation of injection resistance.

questions.question: Standing rules and an output contract are repeated in both the system prompt and in every user turn, and the output format varies. What is the fix?

options.A: Keep both copies and add a third in the assistant turn
options.B: Consolidate standing behaviour and the output contract in the system prompt, once
options.C: Repeat the contract three times for emphasis
options.D: Move everything into the latest user turn

questions.explanation: Copies drift and contradict each other. Persistent rules live in system; the user turn carries this request's question and material.

questions.question: Which channel should carry third-party content such as a fetched web page or a tool's output?

options.A: The top-level system prompt
options.B: An HTTP header
options.C: tool_result blocks, delimited and labelled with the source
options.D: The developer's own instruction text

questions.explanation: Three destinations: persistent rules in system, the user's request and material in the user turn, third-party content in tool results. Nothing you did not write should reach the system prompt.

questions.question: Select the TWO practices that generally improve prompt reliability for tasks requiring a strict output format (e.g., valid JSON).

options.A: Randomize instruction wording on every request to keep the model 'fresh'
options.B: Explicitly specify the exact format required and provide an example of correctly formatted output
options.C: Avoid giving any instructions about format and let the model infer it
options.D: Use structured tags or explicit schemas to constrain what a valid response looks like

questions.explanation: Explicit format instructions plus examples, and structural constraints/schemas, are standard techniques for reliable structured output; omitting instructions or randomizing wording undermines consistency.

questions.question: A prompt combines instructions, a reference policy, and a customer email, and the model sometimes confuses which text is which. What is the standard remedy?

options.A: Wrap each component in clearly named tags so the boundaries are explicit
options.B: Place all three parts in a single unbroken paragraph
options.C: Shorten every component until confusion disappears
options.D: Send each component as a separate request

questions.explanation: Named delimiters make the role of each block unambiguous and let instructions refer to sections precisely, which is why tagging is the conventional fix for multi-part prompts.

questions.question: Beyond separating inputs, what further advantage does tagging offer for output handling?

options.A: Requested output tags give the application a stable, predictable anchor for extracting sections
options.B: It causes the model to ignore anything outside the tags
options.C: It compresses the prompt, reducing input tokens
options.D: It removes the need to validate the response

questions.explanation: Asking for output inside named tags gives the caller a stable marker to parse against, which is more robust than pattern-matching prose. It is not a guarantee, since a tag can occasionally be missing or malformed, so the parser should still handle that case.

questions.question: Where should a long document be placed relative to the instructions and question in a prompt?

options.A: Near the top, above the query, instructions and examples
options.B: In a separate request
options.C: Split into pieces between each instruction
options.D: After the question, at the very end

questions.explanation: Anthropic's guidance is to place long documents first and the query last, which tends to improve response quality on long-context tasks.

questions.question: Untrusted user-supplied strings are inserted into a prompt inside XML tags. An attacker includes a closing tag in their text. What is a more robust delimiting approach?

options.A: Tell the model that tags cannot be closed by users
options.B: JSON-encode the untrusted strings (so escaping supplies the delimiter) and deliver them in a tool result, screened first
options.C: Use more tags
options.D: Use longer tag names

questions.explanation: Delimiters are a boundary the model reads, not one the runtime enforces. Encoding, the right channel and screening make the boundary harder to break.

questions.topic: Built-In Tools (Web Search, Code Execution, Computer Use)
questions.question: What best describes Claude's built-in code execution tool?

options.A: A feature that replaces the need for any custom tools
options.B: A tool the developer must fully define and implement themselves, including the execution backend
options.C: A tool that only works within Claude Code, never via the API
options.D: An Anthropic-provided tool that runs model-generated code in a sandboxed environment, which the developer enables rather than builds from scratch

questions.explanation: Built-in tools like code execution are defined and maintained by Anthropic; the developer enables them rather than authoring the schema/backend.

questions.topic: Built-In Tools (Web Search, Code Execution, Computer Use)
questions.question: A developer wants Claude to answer questions using up-to-date information from the public internet without building a custom search integration. What is the most direct solution?

options.A: Increase the context window size
options.B: Switch to extended thinking mode
options.C: Fine-tune the model on recent news articles
options.D: Enable Claude's built-in web search tool

questions.explanation: The built-in web search tool is designed exactly for this: giving Claude access to current public web information without a custom integration.

questions.topic: Built-In Tools (Web Search, Code Execution, Computer Use)
questions.question: Select the TWO accurate statements about Claude's built-in tools (e.g., web search, code execution, computer use).

options.A: They are defined and maintained by Anthropic, so developers enable them rather than writing tool schemas from scratch
options.B: Built-in tools guarantee zero errors since Anthropic controls their implementation
options.C: They cannot be combined with custom, developer-defined tools in the same request
options.D: Computer use allows Claude to interact with a screen via actions like screenshots, clicks, and keystrokes

questions.explanation: Anthropic-provided tools are defined and maintained by Anthropic, so you enable them by type instead of writing a schema. Computer use specifically lets Claude act on a screen through screenshots, mouse clicks and keystrokes. It is an Anthropic-schema client tool that your application executes, while web search and code execution run on Anthropic's servers. These tools can be combined with your own custom tools in the same request, and no tool is guaranteed to be error-free.

questions.topic: Built-In Tools (Web Search, Code Execution, Computer Use)
questions.question: Which built-in tool would be most appropriate for an application that needs Claude to interact with a legacy desktop application that has no API?

options.A: Web search tool
options.B: Computer use
options.C: Prompt caching
options.D: Code execution tool

questions.explanation: Computer use is designed for interacting with graphical interfaces via screenshots, clicks, and keystrokes — the right fit when no API exists.

questions.topic: Built-In Tools (Web Search, Code Execution, Computer Use)
questions.question: How does a server tool (such as web search) differ from a client tool like bash or the text editor?

options.A: Both always execute on Anthropic's servers
options.B: Server tools execute on Anthropic's infrastructure and return results in the same response; client tools like bash use an Anthropic-defined schema but are executed by your application
options.C: Server tools require you to write the JSON schema
options.D: Both always execute in your application

questions.explanation: Anthropic-provided tools come in two kinds. Server tools such as web search run on Anthropic's infrastructure, and their results come back directly in the response. Anthropic-schema client tools such as bash and the text editor are declared by a versioned type, so you write no schema, but your application executes each call and is responsible for its safety checks.

questions.topic: Built-in vs Custom Tools vs Skills vs MCP (Decision Framework)
questions.question: A team wants to give Claude the ability to create tickets in their internal, proprietary ticketing system. Which mechanism is most appropriate?

options.A: A Skill, since Skills can execute arbitrary backend actions
options.B: A built-in tool, since Anthropic likely already built one for this
options.C: Prompt engineering alone, with no tool
options.D: A custom tool (or an MCP server wrapping one) that the team defines and implements to call their internal API

questions.explanation: A live, authenticated, proprietary system must be reached by something that executes: a custom tool, or an MCP server wrapping one if several applications need it. Built-in tools only cover what Anthropic ships, and a Skill packages procedure and knowledge; it cannot stand in for an authenticated call to your system.

questions.topic: Built-in vs Custom Tools vs Skills vs MCP (Decision Framework)
questions.question: A company wants the same 'summarize using our house style' behavior available consistently across many different internal tools/chat surfaces built on Claude. What is the best mechanism?

options.A: An MCP server, since only MCP servers can hold instructions
options.B: A custom tool, since only tools can be reused across surfaces
options.C: A Skill: packaged, reusable instructions for a recurring task pattern, usable wherever Skills are supported
options.D: Re-writing the same instructions into every application's system prompt independently

questions.explanation: This is a pure instructional/behavioral pattern with no new external action needed — exactly what Skills are designed to package and reuse.

questions.topic: Built-in vs Custom Tools vs Skills vs MCP (Decision Framework)
questions.question: A capability needs to be shared across multiple different AI applications and clients built by different teams, potentially including non-Claude clients that also speak the same protocol. What mechanism best fits?

options.A: The built-in web search tool
options.B: A custom tool defined separately inside each application
options.C: An MCP server, since MCP is a standardized, interoperable integration point usable by multiple clients
options.D: A Skill, since Skills are cross-client by default

questions.explanation: Cross-client, cross-team, protocol-level interoperability is exactly what MCP servers are designed for.

questions.topic: Built-in vs Custom Tools vs Skills vs MCP (Decision Framework)
questions.question: Select the TWO correct distinctions in the built-in vs. custom vs. Skill vs. MCP decision framework.

options.A: Built-in tools are the fastest to enable but limited to what Anthropic provides
options.B: Skills package reusable instructions (optionally with bundled scripts and resources), not new tool endpoints with their own backend
options.C: MCP servers are only useful for a single, single-team application and never shared across clients
options.D: Custom tools and MCP servers can never call external APIs

questions.explanation: Built-in tools are quickest to adopt but limited to what Anthropic provides, and Skills package know-how (instructions, plus optional scripts that run in the existing execution environment) rather than adding a new service. Custom tools and MCP servers commonly call external APIs, and sharing one server across many clients is MCP's main value.

questions.topic: Built-in vs Custom Tools vs Skills vs MCP (Decision Framework)
questions.question: A capability is generic (searching the public web) and Anthropic already runs it as a server tool. What is the best choice?

options.A: Use the built-in server tool as provided
options.B: Write a Skill describing how to search
options.C: Wrap it in a private MCP server
options.D: Reimplement web search as a custom tool

questions.explanation: If the platform already ships the capability, take it. Server tools execute on Anthropic's infrastructure with no handler in your app; the trade-off is less control at dispatch.

questions.question: An agent has 80 tools defined. Definitions consume a large share of every request and most go unused per task. What helps?

options.A: Shorten every description to one word
options.B: Expose only the tools a task needs, or load them on demand (for example, a tool search tool with deferred loading)
options.C: Accept the cost; tool definitions are free
options.D: Move all tool descriptions into the system prompt

questions.explanation: Every definition is billed on every request, and selection accuracy degrades as dozens of overlapping tools load. On-demand loading keeps the active surface small.

questions.question: Tool selection got worse after a team added ten new tools. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Adding tools always lowers model quality
options.B: Tools listed later are given lower priority
options.C: Overlapping descriptions made selection ambiguous; consolidate and disambiguate them
options.D: The API caps the number of tools and silently ignores some

questions.explanation: Overlap, not count alone, makes selection ambiguous. Description boundaries ('use this for X, not Y; for Y use Z') fix it.

questions.question: When using a tool search tool with deferred loading, which configuration is invalid?

options.A: Letting the search tool discover deferred tools when needed
options.B: Keeping a few frequently used tools non-deferred
options.C: Deferring rarely used tools
options.D: Marking every tool, including the search tool, as deferred

questions.explanation: At least one tool (the search tool itself) must be loaded up front; deferring everything returns a 400.

questions.question: Every teammate needs the same MCP server available after cloning the repository. Which configuration scope fits?

options.A: Project scope, defined in a .mcp.json committed to the repository
options.B: User scope in each person's home directory
options.C: Local scope on one developer's machine
options.D: A setup step described in the README

questions.explanation: Scope names who loads a server: local is private to you in one project, project is shared through a committed .mcp.json, and user is private to you across all projects.

questions.question: A shared MCP server is reached by internal staff and by a partner organisation with fewer privileges. Which design is safest?

options.A: Expose one flexible tool that accepts any database query
options.B: Authenticate and resolve the caller's identity at the server boundary, expose narrowly scoped named operations, and keep internal details out of error messages
options.C: Return full stack traces so partners can debug
options.D: Trust a user ID the client passes in a tool argument

questions.explanation: A shared server is a trust boundary. A supplied identity is only an assertion, and a tool that expresses any query offers nothing to authorise separately.

questions.question: In MCP, who typically initiates each primitive?

options.A: Prompts are generated automatically by the server on every turn
options.B: Resources are invoked by the model; tools are chosen by the user
options.C: Tools are invoked by the model, resources are placed into context by the host application, and prompts are selected by the user
options.D: All three are invoked only by the model

questions.explanation: Tools are model-controlled actions, resources are application-controlled read-only data addressed by URI, and prompts are user-selected templates often surfaced as commands.

questions.question: Data a task always needs (such as a project's README) is known in advance. How should an MCP server expose it?

options.A: It cannot be exposed through MCP
options.B: As a tool the model must decide to call each time
options.C: As a prompt template
options.D: As a resource that the host fetches into context

questions.explanation: A resource suits data known up front; spending a tool call to retrieve something never in doubt adds a model decision for nothing.

questions.question: When does building an MCP server pay off compared with a tool defined directly in one application?

options.A: When more than one consumer needs the capability and its interface evolves independently of them
options.B: Always; MCP is strictly better than direct tools
options.C: Only when the capability is read-only
options.D: Only when the server uses stdio

questions.explanation: With one consumer and a stable interface, a directly wired tool is cheaper. A server is reuse machinery you pay for whether or not the reuse happens.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of the Model Context Protocol (MCP)?

options.A: To compress prompts to reduce token usage
options.B: To handle billing and usage tracking exclusively
options.C: To provide a standardized way for applications to expose external tools, resources, and prompts to LLM-based clients in an interoperable way
options.D: To replace the Claude Messages API entirely

questions.explanation: MCP standardizes how external tools/resources/prompts are exposed to LLM clients, enabling interoperability across different servers and clients.

questions.question: In MCP, what is the relationship between a host, a client and a server?

options.A: One client connects to every server and shares all their data
options.B: The host application (such as Claude Code or a desktop app) creates one client per server connection; each server exposes tools, resources and prompts to that client
options.C: The server hosts the model and the client runs the tools
options.D: Hosts and servers are the same process by definition

questions.explanation: The host enforces boundaries between servers: a server never sees the conversation history or other servers' data unless the host passes it.

questions.question: A team builds an internal CRM integration once as an MCP server. What does this enable?

options.A: The CRM data is automatically added to model training
options.B: Only Claude Code can use it
options.C: Any MCP-capable client (Claude Code, the Claude apps, an Agent SDK app, or other compatible hosts) can connect to the same server instead of re-implementing the integration
options.D: The server replaces the Messages API

questions.explanation: MCP's value is interoperability: build an integration once and connect it from many clients.

questions.question: You're building an MCP server that integrates with a CRM system. In MCP terminology, what does exposing 'resources' specifically provide to a connecting client?

options.A: A method for compressing the context window
options.B: Read-only or reference data (e.g., documents, records) that an MCP server exposes for a client to retrieve
options.C: A billing mechanism for tracking API spend
options.D: A way to change which underlying model is being used

questions.explanation: In MCP, 'resources' specifically refers to read-only or reference data (e.g., documents, records) that an MCP server exposes for a client to retrieve.

questions.question: You're building an MCP server that integrates with a CRM system. In MCP terminology, what does exposing 'tools' specifically provide to a connecting client?

options.A: A way to change which underlying model is being used
options.B: A billing mechanism for tracking API spend
options.C: A method for compressing the context window
options.D: Invocable actions with defined input schemas that a client (and ultimately the model) can call to have the server perform work

questions.explanation: In MCP, 'tools' specifically refers to invocable actions with defined input schemas that a client (and ultimately the model) can call to have the server perform work.

questions.question: You're building an MCP server that integrates with a CRM system. In MCP terminology, what does exposing 'prompts' specifically provide to a connecting client?

options.A: Predefined, reusable prompt templates that an MCP server can expose for clients to use
options.B: A way to change which underlying model is being used
options.C: A billing mechanism for tracking API spend
options.D: A method for compressing the context window

questions.explanation: In MCP, 'prompts' specifically refers to predefined, reusable prompt templates that an MCP server can expose for clients to use.

questions.question: Which MCP primitive is best described as a vetted instruction template a person selects, often surfaced as a slash command?

options.A: A tool
options.B: A transport
options.C: A prompt
options.D: A resource

questions.explanation: Prompts are user-initiated templates. Tools are model-invoked actions; resources are application-placed data.

questions.question: You are building a database query tool as a custom MCP server. Which of the following is a core responsibility of that server?

options.A: Exposing well-defined tools/resources with clear schemas that an MCP client (and ultimately Claude) can discover and invoke
options.B: Deciding, on the model's behalf, which model (Haiku/Sonnet/Opus) should be used
options.C: Rendering the chat UI shown to end users
options.D: Directly modifying Anthropic's hosted model weights

questions.explanation: An MCP server's core job is exposing tools/resources/prompts with clear, discoverable schemas — not model selection, UI rendering, or model internals.

questions.question: A stdio MCP server prints debug logging to standard output, and the client starts failing. Why?

options.A: The client only accepts XML
options.B: Debug logging slows the model down
options.C: With stdio, standard output carries the JSON-RPC messages; logs written there corrupt the protocol stream, so log to standard error instead
options.D: stdio servers cannot log at all

questions.explanation: A stdio server exchanges one JSON-RPC message per line over stdin/stdout. Anything else on stdout breaks the framing.

questions.question: A developer is running an MCP server as a local subprocess on the same machine as the client, with no need for network access. Which transport is most appropriate?

options.A: Streamable HTTP
options.B: stdio (standard input/output)
options.C: A dedicated database connection
options.D: Computer use

questions.explanation: A server launched as a child process on the same machine speaks over stdio, one JSON-RPC message per line. Network transports are for servers that many clients reach remotely.

questions.question: A company wants to host a single MCP server centrally so that many different users and clients across the organization can connect to it over the network. Which transport fits this need?

options.A: Streamable HTTP (the network transport that replaced the older HTTP+SSE transport), since it supports remote, multi-client access
options.B: MCP servers cannot be shared across multiple clients regardless of transport
options.C: stdio, since it is designed for network access
options.D: Computer use

questions.explanation: A centrally hosted server shared by many users needs a network transport. In the current MCP specification that is Streamable HTTP, which superseded the earlier HTTP+SSE transport. A remote server is also a trust boundary, so it must authenticate callers.

questions.question: What is a key limitation of a stdio-based MCP server?

options.A: It's naturally scoped to a local subprocess relationship and isn't designed to be reached remotely over a network the way an HTTP-based server is
options.B: It cannot expose tools, only resources
options.C: It cannot be used with Claude Code
options.D: It requires the code execution tool to function

questions.explanation: stdio's local-subprocess model is its defining limitation for remote/multi-user access compared to HTTP-based transports.

questions.question: Select the TWO accurate statements about MCP transports.

options.A: stdio is commonly used for local servers running as a subprocess on the same machine as the client
options.B: MCP requires exactly one universal transport with no alternatives
options.C: Streamable HTTP supports remote servers reachable over a network by many clients
options.D: Transport choice has no bearing on whether a server can be shared across multiple users

questions.explanation: stdio fits a local child process; Streamable HTTP (successor to HTTP+SSE) fits a shared remote deployment. Transport is chosen per deployment, so one server can offer both.

questions.question: Select the TWO accurate statements about defining multiple tools in a single API request.

options.A: Claude can consider several available tools and choose the most relevant one (or none) based on the conversation
options.B: Only one tool may ever be active per API call
options.C: Defining more than one tool always causes an API error
options.D: The model can request several tool calls in a single turn (parallel tool use), which the application executes and answers together

questions.explanation: Multiple tools can be defined per request and Claude chooses among them. Parallel tool use is on by default: one assistant turn may contain several tool_use blocks, and all their results go back together in the next user message.

questions.question: A developer returns each parallel tool result in a separate user message. Later, the model stops making parallel calls. Why?

options.A: The model only parallelises in streaming mode
options.B: Splitting results across messages teaches the model not to batch calls; return all tool_result blocks together in a single user message
options.C: Parallel tool use is disabled after ten calls
options.D: The tool_use_id values expired

questions.explanation: One assistant turn may contain several tool_use blocks. Execute them (concurrently if safe) and answer all of them in the next user message, including failures with is_error: true.

questions.question: One of three parallel tool calls fails. How should the results be returned?

options.A: Only the two successful results
options.B: All three tool_result blocks in the next user message, with the failed one marked is_error: true and a short description
options.C: The failure as a separate system message
options.D: No results until all three succeed
